activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
Brandon had the video open on his phone for the third time when the automatic doors of the library sighed shut behind him. In the clip, a warehouse roof sagged under floodwater while a man's voice shouted about collapsed beams, and the caption beneath it named a company in town, Halloran Freight, and said the flood had happened "last night." Forty thousand people had already shared it. Brandon's father worked at the bank two doors down from Halloran's yard, and Brandon had been about to forward it to the family group chat, and then to the soccer team chat, and then, if he was honest, to Nelly, who would appreciate the drama. Instead he had paused, because his father had once mentioned, over burnt toast, that Halloran carried the bank's loan and that people liked to denigrate the owner for sport, and Brandon had looked up "denigrate" and decided it was a word that applied to him more often than he liked.

He found Nelly and Jensen at the table by the window, guarding a heap of highlighters like dragons over gold. Jensen was supposed to be studying for the chemistry retake. Instead he was watching the same video.

"Halloran's gone under," Jensen said, not looking up. "My cousin says insolvency by Christmas. Flood like that, no insurance, done."

"My dad says the loan's fine," Brandon said.

"Your dad would say that. He's the bank."

"He's a junior analyst, Jensen, he doesn't guard the vault with a sword."

Mr. Morin passed behind them with a trolley of returns, and paused, because librarians pause the way cats do, at exactly the wrong moment. "That video," he said, "is on every screen in this building. Including, I regret to report, mine."

"Is it real?" Nelly asked him.

"I don't answer questions I can't answer," Mr. Morin said, which was his way of saying figure it out yourselves, and he rolled the trolley on toward the front desk with what Brandon considered an unnecessary amount of dignity.

Brandon sat down. He had something in his back pocket besides his phone, which was a Saturday two months ago at his father's office, killing time in a swivel chair while his father finished a call. A colleague at the next desk had spun her monitor around and said, watch this, and clicked a little button in her browser. "It's called InVID-WeVerify," she had said. "Some European Union-funded project. My sister swears by it." Then she'd fed it a video and it had chopped the clip into still frames, key frames she called them, and each one could be dragged into a reverse image search, and the first result had shown the same footage from three years earlier on a news site in another language. The colleague had laughed so hard she'd had to put down her coffee. Brandon had laughed too, mostly at her laugh, and had forgotten all of it until now.

"Give me the library computer," he said.

"You have a phone," said Jensen.

"Your face has a phone. Give me the computer." Brandon logged in at the catalogue terminal, installed the plugin, which took two minutes and one false start that Nelly narrated as "he's broken the library," and dropped the video link in. The screen filled with a grid of stills: the sagging roof, the shouting man, a green dumpster at the frame's edge, a half-visible license plate. Key frames. He dragged the dumpster one into a reverse image search first, because a sagging roof looked like every sagging roof ever filmed, but a dumpster with a specific scorch mark on it was a fingerprint.

The results loaded. A regional news article, dated four years back, from a town whose name Brandon could pronounce only syllable by syllable. Same dumpster, same scorch, same man mid-shout. Nelly leaned in so far her ponytail touched the keyboard.

"So the caption's a lie," she said slowly, "and the flood's real, but it's somebody else's flood."

"Four years old and two countries over," Brandon said. He felt the particular warmth of being right, and then the smaller, colder feeling underneath it, which was that he had been twenty seconds from sharing the thing himself, and that if the stills had matched a genuinely local flood, the plugin would have told him nothing about whether Halloran could survive it. The tool could catch a lie. It couldn't certify the truth. He sat with that for a moment, cursor blinking on the fake caption, and decided he was okay with the residue of uncertainty, though he'd keep it off the group chat.

"You should comment on it," Jensen said. "Say it's fake. Denounce it."

"If I comment, forty thousand people see my name next to a warehouse, and half of them decide my dad's bank is rotten too." Brandon had read enough comment sections to know the deleterious arithmetic: one correction, thirty arguments, zero conversions. "I'll message the couple of people who actually matter. My dad. Maybe Mr. Halloran, he follows me for some reason."

Mr. Morin reappeared without his trolley, set a printed page face-down beside the keyboard, and said, "For when you finish not breaking my computer." It was a bookmark-sized flyer about evaluating sources, clearly printed in 2011, with a clip-art magnifying glass. Brandon turned it over, turned it back, and slid it into his pocket anyway.

"Collectible," he said.

"Everything is, eventually," said Mr. Morin.

Jensen opened his mouth, closed it, and pulled the chemistry binder toward himself like a man accepting a sentence. Nelly was already screenshotting the key frames for her own folder, which she labeled, out loud as she typed, "Evidence, Volume One." Brandon hit send on the message to his father: old video, other country, check with the loan officer before the cousin does.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Psychologist Robert Zajonc's 1968 experiments showed the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often.
story:
The last boxes went into the garage by ten, and the movers were coming at seven, which gave Victor one final night in a house that already looked like a stranger's. Sylas and Brodie had come over with a twelve-pack of root beer and a borrowed projector, and they were taping the bedsheet to the living room wall where the television used to be. "We're watching the game on a bedsheet," Brodie said, smoothing a wrinkle with his palm. "This is the saddest thing I've ever done, and I once watched Mr. Gagnon's car get towed with him running behind it in slippers."

"It's not sad," Sylas said. "It's resourceful. Victor, tell him it's resourceful." But Victor was looking at the rectangle of unfaded paint where the television had stood for eleven years, a shape slightly brighter than the wall around it, like a photograph of an object that wasn't there anymore. He said it was resourceful anyway.

They watched half the game on the sheet, and at halftime Sylas pulled his phone out and started reading, which he did when he was trying not to say something. "You know what my cousin told me," he finally said. "When they moved to Belleville. Psychologist Robert Zajonc did these experiments in 1968. People tend to like things more just because they've seen them more often. It's called the mere-exposure effect." He set the phone face down on the floor between them as if it were evidence. "She said she hated the bus route in Belleville, like genuinely hated it, and a month later it was the thing she missed when she visited her grandma."

"So the new town just has to be boring at me for a month," Victor said, "and I'll like it by accident."

"Basically."

Brodie flopped backward onto the dead grass of the carpet, where the rug used to be. "That's the most depressing thing I've ever heard. Liking something because you're trapped next to it. That's not liking, that's surrender." He pointed at the ceiling. "If I got exiled to some town in the middle of nowhere I would excoriate it every single day. Loudly. In writing. So it couldn't sneak up on me." He was joking the way he always joked, arms wide, but Victor noticed he said "if I got exiled" instead of "if you got exiled," and they both noticed it too, and nobody said anything for a second.

The trouble was that Victor could already feel it working on him in reverse. The new town had a name, Herron Creek, and a map he'd unfolded so many times the creases had gone soft and white. He'd traced the route from the house to the school, from the house to a library he'd never entered, from the house to a diner called the Ridge that he'd already decided was terrible based on one photograph. And in the last week he had caught himself thinking of the diner's crooked sign almost fondly, the way you think of a classmate's crooked tooth. Whether that was the thing Sylas's cousin described, or just his brain making the best of happenstance, he couldn't tell, and the not-knowing bothered him more than either answer would have. If liking could arrive by mere repetition, then maybe the fondness he felt for this carpet, this staircase, this particular dip in the kitchen floor had never been about the house at all. Maybe he'd been loving things on a schedule and calling it a home.

"Say something," Brodie said from the floor. "You're doing your thinking face and it's freaking me out."

"I think both of you are right," Victor said slowly. "It's probably true that I'll end up liking it, and it's probably also true that doesn't mean anything. Except." He picked up the projector's remote and turned it over in his hands. "Except my dad says nobody in Herron Creek knows me, and everybody here knows me, and if Zajonc is right, then in about a month there'll be kids there who've seen me enough times to like me, and they'll think it's because of who I am. And maybe it will be. You can't really tell the two apart from the inside." Sylas opened his mouth, and Victor held up a hand. "I'm not saying that like it's sagacious. I'm saying it keeps me up at night."

The projector hummed. On the sheet, the halftime show went to commercial and then to commercial again.

"Okay," Brodie said finally, sitting up. "Then we make you unmissable. Sylas, get the marker from the kitchen. The fat one." He pulled the bedsheet down off the wall, snapping one corner free of the tape, and spread it flat across the floor. "You're taking this. On the bus. Tomorrow. Everybody signs it, and you hang it up in the new room, and every time you see it, that's exposure too." He uncapped the marker with his teeth and wrote his name in the lower corner, huge, taking up a scandalous amount of sheet. "There. Now you have to remember me, whether you like it or not."

Sylas took the marker next, and knelt down close to the fabric, and Victor watched him hesitate over the empty white space, deciding how big to make it.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
The library at four o'clock had a crepuscular feeling even with all the lights on, the tall windows letting in a thin grey light that made the carpet look older than it was. Xavier had claimed the table by the periodicals because it was far from the circulation desk, and for two weeks it had been his. Now Cash had dragged over a chair without asking, and Josiah was spreading out a photocopied page like he owned the building.

"Book club," Josiah said, as though this explained anything. "Ms. Virtanen started it. You're in it. She told me to tell you."

"I'm not in anything."

"You're holding the copy she made for you." Josiah nodded at the packet under Xavier's elbow, which was, in fact, a copy with Xavier's name on it in Ms. Virtanen's looping hand. He had not noticed. He had been reading the same paragraph of Jane Eyre for forty minutes.

Cash cleared his throat in the way of someone about to perform. He read aloud from the packet, slowly, with the gravity of a boy who had practiced: "'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.'" He set the page down. "First section. Communist Manifesto, 1848. Marx and Engels just come out and say it, like a thesis statement."

"That's the whole first line?" Xavier asked.

"That's how it opens. First section of the whole thing."

Xavier looked at the paragraph of Jane Eyre he had been failing to read, and something in it rearranged itself. Jane, a penniless orphan, living in a rich man's house, being told she is less than the servants because she is not paid to be there at all. Governesses occupied a slot that fit no category, which was, he suspected, the entire point of governesses in novels. "So if class struggle is the engine of everything," he said slowly, "then Jane's problem isn't that she's sad. It's that she's a have-not surrounded by haves, and marriage is the only ladder they'll let her touch."

Josiah leaned back. "That's bleak."

"That's the lens," Xavier said, and was surprised at how easily the phrase arrived, as if he had been carrying it unassembled.

Ms. Virtanen passed behind them with a cart of returns and said nothing, which Xavier understood as her highest form of approval. She had assigned the lenses the way a chemistry teacher assigns reagents: here is feminism, here is Marxism, see what changes color. He had assumed he would have to choose one. Now, turning the page, he found he didn't. When Rochester disguises himself as a gypsy woman to read the fortunes of his guests, he is performing a class he can put on and take off, which Jane cannot, and performing a gender he also controls, which the actual women in the room do not. The trick only works because he holds all the power in both categories at once.

"Wait," Cash said, watching Xavier's face do something. "Say that out loud."

"He dresses as a gypsy. So he's slumming, class-wise, and cross-dressing, gender-wise, and he can stop being both whenever he wants. Nobody else at that party can." Xavier tapped the page. "The two lenses aren't fighting. They're pointing at the same man."

Josiah considered this with the expression of someone tasting something he could not yet name. "Okay, but does it fit the manifesto thing, though? One class against another, all through history? A governess isn't exactly the proletariat."

"I don't know," Xavier said, and found he liked saying it. "Maybe the novel is the exception that tests it. Maybe Marx would say she's petty bourgeois because she's educated. Or maybe she's proof the whole history-of-class-struggles frame leaves out people who fall between the classes, and the novel knows it even if the manifesto doesn't."

"That's a hedge," said Cash.

"That's a considered position," said Josiah, who had clearly also been listening to Ms. Virtanen.

Here was the twist, though it did not arrive as a twist, only as a fact Xavier had failed to check: flipping to the back of the packet, he found the sheet Ms. Virtanen had tucked in for the next session, a page of the manifesto's later section, where the authors admitted that their opening claim had hitherto-existing exceptions of its own, societies the frame did not yet cover. They had flagged it themselves. Marx and Engels had gotten to Xavier's uncertainty a hundred and seventy years early, and had left a note, which he was now reading by the light of a window going properly dark.

"Ms. Virtanen," he called, before he could decide whether to. She turned the cart around. "Did you put this page in on purpose? Because it says basically what I just said."

She looked at the sheet, then at him, and titrated her smile to something very small. "The next meeting is Thursday," she said, and pushed the cart toward the front desk, where the cashier, or rather the student aide, was shelving holds under a lamp that buzzed.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
story:
The two articles had been open on Jade's laptop for three days, and the kitchen table had slowly filled around them: a mug gone cold, two granola wrappers, a printout bristling with pink sticky notes, and, at the far end, her half-written review, fourteen sentences long and stalled. Both articles asked the same question, whether a later school start time improved adolescent attention, and both had found an effect, but the second one, by a team she'd never heard of, kept waving a number at her: p = 0.05. She had written, in the sentence she was now ashamed of, that this made the study's conclusion "95 percent likely to be right." It had sounded confident when she typed it. It sounded worse every time she read it.

Jaylen arrived at six with his backpack and the last two slices of pizza from wherever he'd been before, and he dropped into the chair across from her without asking, because that was the arrangement on nights like this. He was supposed to be doing calculus, and for a while he actually was, hunched over a worksheet on proof by induction, copying out the base case and muttering the word "lemma" at the ceiling as if the ceiling owed him one. "It's just a little theorem you prove first so the big one works," he said, catching her look. "But they won't let you call it a theorem. They make you call it a lemma, like it's a servant."

Jade slid her laptop across the table. "Read my third paragraph. Tell me if it sounds smart or if it sounds like I'm bluffing."

He read it with pizza in one hand. He got to the ninety-five percent sentence and stopped chewing. "Wait. Where'd you get that number?"

"From the p-value. It's right there. Point oh five. That's five percent chance of being wrong, so ninety-five percent chance of being right."

Jaylen set the pizza down, which for Jaylen was a serious gesture. "That's what p means?"

"I think so." Her heart had begun to palpitate in the small, irritating way it did before a test she hadn't studied for. "That's what everyone says it means. Hugh said it means the study's basically proven."

"Hugh also said the AP Chem exam was cancelled that time." Jaylen turned the laptop back toward her and tapped the screen, once, on the number. "The problem is I read a thing about this, like a footnote in my stats unit, and it said the opposite of what you wrote. I don't remember the wording. But it was definitely the opposite."

She wanted to tell him he was wrong. She wanted it so much that she noticed the wanting, which was a habit Ms. Ong had trained into her class in September: when you feel yourself defending a sentence instead of checking it, check it. The review was due at eight the next morning, uploaded to the class portal, no extensions, and this sentence was load-bearing; it was the hinge of her whole argument that the second study deserved more weight than the first.

The first article had run a huge sample across forty schools and published its raw data, but its writing was lugubrious, forty pages of hedge and qualification that seemed embarrassed to have found anything. The second was brisk and clean and certain, which was exactly why she'd trusted it, and now that she looked again at its certainty, with Jaylen's frown across the table like weather moving in, she saw that the number doing all the work was the one she couldn't actually explain. She pulled up the search bar. Her fingers hovered. If Jaylen was right, the sentence was wrong, and if the sentence was wrong, the paragraph was wrong, and if the paragraph was wrong, the position she'd staked out, that the second study was the stronger of the two, was standing on a misread number.

She found it in a stats primer, then in a second one, and the wording was the same in both, plain as a door. A p-value was the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect. It was not the probability that the hypothesis was true. She read it aloud, slowly, and watched Jaylen's face do the thing where confusion turns into something almost delighted. "So it's backwards from what you wrote," he said. "It's not even about the hypothesis. It's like, if the world were boring, how weird would your data be."

"How weird would my data be," Jade repeated, writing it on the margin of her printout. The first article, she now saw, had reported a p-value far smaller and had still hedged, had still said the effect might not generalize, and that hedge wasn't cowardice; it was someone who understood that a small p-value closed off one boring possibility without opening the door to certainty. The second article had dressed up the same kind of number as proof.

She cut the sentence. She cut the sentence after it too, and the one claiming the second study was "basically proven," and for a bad ten minutes the paragraph was just a wound of deleted clauses. Then she rebuilt it around what she could honestly say: that the two studies agreed on the direction of the effect, that the second's tighter statistics ruled out chance more strongly, and that neither could tell her how likely the hypothesis itself was to be true, which was the question every reader actually cared about. Her position softened from "the second is stronger" to "the second is stronger for one purpose and shakier for another," and she sat with that for a moment, testing whether it felt like weakness or like the truth. It felt like the truth, with a hole in the middle of it that she could see clearly and would say so.

At eleven she read the final draft aloud while Jaylen, long done with calculus, graded his own homework with theatrical despair. When she finished, he pushed the pizza box aside and rested his chin on his hand. "So what's the takeaway?"

"There isn't one clean takeaway. That's the takeaway." She closed the laptop and looked at the table, at the sticky notes and the cold mug and the margin where she'd written how weird would my data be. "I'm probably going to get a worse grade for saying I don't know the thing everyone pretends to know."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Because several codons can code for the same amino acid, some single-base mutations change nothing in the finished protein; these are called silent mutations.
story:
Elijah had agreed to help at the community garden every Saturday until mid-June, which his mother called character-building and which Elijah called a bargain, because Ms. Nwosu had let him store his biology textbook in the shed with the seed packets. He was failing biology, or nearly, and the makeup exam was on Monday, and the shed smelled of damp earth and basil in a way that made the material feel almost survivable. On this particular Saturday he sat on an upturned crate with the book open on his knees, drawing arrows in the margin with a pencil stub, while Laetitia sorted tomato stakes and Faisal did what Faisal did best, which was lie across the wheelbarrow like a saturnine prince pretending he had been forced into exile.

"If you're going to loom," Elijah said, "loom usefully. Quiz me."

Faisal held up a hand without opening his eyes. "Transcription. Go."

"DNA to mRNA. The cell copies the gene, letter by letter, except T becomes U. Then the copy leaves the nucleus and gets read in threes. Each three-letter word is a codon, and each codon means one amino acid. The amino acids get chained together and folded, and that's the protein."

"Translation," said Faisal, with the air of a man conceding a point to a rival monarch.

Laetitia dropped her stakes and came over, wiping her hands on her jeans. "Okay, but explain it like I'm a plant. Ms. Nwosu says you learn things better when you teach them."

"That is not a scientific claim," Elijah said, but he stood up anyway, because she had that look. He pointed at the long bed of beans Ms. Nwosu had planted in rows. "Fine. The seed packet is the DNA, the master copy, kept safe in the shed. Transcription is me copying the instructions onto a label. Translation is you reading the label and actually putting the seeds in the ground at the right spacing. The finished bean row is the protein."

"So the label is a transliteration," Laetitia said slowly. "Same information, different alphabet."

Elijah blinked. He had been going to say "copy," but hers was better, and he told her so, and Faisal made a retching noise from the wheelbarrow, which they both ignored.

Then Laetitia, flipping through the book while Elijah hunted for the watering can, stopped at the page with the worked example. "Wait. This is broken. Look. Question fourteen changes one letter in the DNA, and the answer key says the protein comes out exactly the same. Exactly the same. That can't be right. If you change a word, you change the word."

Elijah took the book back and looked. She was right about the letters: one base swapped, the mRNA different by one letter, and yet the final protein printed in the answer key was identical, amino acid for amino acid. He felt the specific panic of a student who suspects the universe of containing an error. He checked the codon chart at the back of the book, running his finger down the rows, muttering the letters aloud.

"AAA and AAG," he said. "Both code for the same amino acid. Both of them. And look, CCT and CCC, same thing again." He laughed, a short disbelieving laugh, and sat back down on the crate so fast he nearly missed it. "The code has backups. You can change a letter and the sentence still reads the same, because several different codons can mean the same amino acid. The mutation changes nothing in the finished protein."

"Then what's it even called," Laetitia said, "a mutation that does nothing?" She turned the page, and there in the margin, in the handwriting of some earlier owner of the textbook, were the words. "Silent mutations," she read aloud. "That's the word. Somebody wrote it right here."

"A mutation that keeps quiet," Faisal said from the wheelbarrow, finally opening one eye. "The polite kind. Changes its clothes and says nothing at the dinner table."

"You're describing subterfuge," said Elijah, "and yes, actually, that's exactly it. Except there's no scheming. It just happens that the code is built with this slack in it." He copied the margin note into his own notebook, then, feeling grand, drew a small bean plant next to it.

Ms. Nwosu came around the corner of the shed with a trug of chives and regarded the three of them: the boy on the crate waving a textbook, the girl reading a margin, the boy draped over her wheelbarrow like an unfurled tarp. "Whatever it is," she said, "you're paying for the wheelbarrow if it bends."

"It's science, Ms. Nwosu," Elijah said. "Silent science."

She set down the trug. "Then do it loudly somewhere useful. The carrots want thinning, and you can explain your silence to them."

Elijah stood, tucked the book under his arm, and pulled on his gloves. "Carrots," he announced to the row, kneeling in the dirt, "as you were."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and was first called SEQUEL.
story:
The kitchen table at Samantha's house had become a workstation: two laptops, a bowl of pistachios, and a printout of the assignment that Ms. Holloway had handed out on Friday. Find the customers who have never placed an order. Seth read it three times on the bus and twice more here, and the words still sat oddly in his mouth. It seemed strange that a question could sound so simple and then hide.

"Left join," Kathryn said, spinning her pen between her fingers. "You join customers to orders, and the ones with nothing come back empty on the order side. Then you filter for the empty." She said it the way she said most things, as though the world were a debate she was currently winning.

Samantha, who had sequestered herself at the far end of the table with her own screen turned away from them, looked up. "It's pronounced S-Q-L. You spell it out. Everyone in my brother's office spells it out."

"Everyone I've ever heard says sequel." Kathryn's voice took on that pugnacious edge she got when she suspected she was about to be right. "Sequel. Like the movie."

Seth, who had been quietly typing, paused. "Maybe you're both right." Both girls turned, and he felt the familiar flush of having spoken before he had finished thinking. "I mean, maybe it started as one thing and turned into the other." He pulled up a search page and typed the letters in, half expecting the internet to shrug. Instead the answer came back immediately, plain and definitive, and he read it twice before saying it aloud. "It was developed at IBM in the early 1970s, by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce. And it was first called SEQUEL."

The kitchen went quiet in the particular way it does when an argument loses both of its sides at once. Kathryn stared at him. "So I'm right."

"So you're both right," Samantha said, and something in her face had softened, which surprised him. "It was called SEQUEL, so the people saying sequel are saying the original name. And the people spelling it out are saying what it became." She tapped the table. "I like that. Two names for the same thing, and neither one is wrong."

Seth thought of his grandfather's garage, of an afternoon two summers ago when the old man had tried to teach him to solder. The iron smelled like hot metal and pine from the shelf above, and his grandfather had held his hand steady over the joint and said, "The secret is that you're not melting the solder. You're heating the metal, and the solder follows the heat." Seth had ruined three joints before he understood, and then the fourth had flowed like water finding a channel. He had walked home that evening feeling as though he had been let in on a small, private physics. This felt similar, sitting here: two tables, customers and orders, and the question of how to find an absence. You couldn't ask for nothing directly. You had to ask for everything and then look at which rows came back half empty.

He typed it out carefully, narrating for Kathryn, who had pulled her chair around to watch. "Select star from customers, left join orders on the customer ID." He ran it. The table filled: dozens of rows, most with order numbers attached, and there, scattered like beads dropped in grass, four customers with nothing but blank space where their orders should be. Samantha leaned across the pistachios to see.

"Those four," she said. "Marcia Delano. The Wexford account."

"Never ordered anything," Seth said. "They exist in one table and not the other, and the join is how you catch it." He scrolled slowly, wondering whether the people at IBM, all those years ago, had known they were building something that could answer a question about absence. Maybe they had needed it for exactly this. Maybe somebody in 1974 had a list of customers and a list of orders and the same itch at the back of the mind. He didn't say any of that out loud. Some thoughts were better kept as thoughts, at least until they hardened.

Kathrina was already copying his query into her own file, adapting it, changing the column names to match the sample database Ms. Holloway had posted. She was quick about it, unembarrassed, the way she was quick at everything. As a counterpoint to her earlier certainty, her quiet borrowing of his answer said more than an apology would have. Seth watched her run it, watched her four empty rows appear, and felt a small, warm flare of something he couldn't quite name. Pride was too strong. Satisfaction was too flat. Maybe it was just the pleasure of a thing working.

"I'm still going to say sequel," Kathryn said, closing her laptop halfway. "Now I have a reason."

"You have a history," Samantha said. "That's not the same as a reason." She reached across and stole one of his pistachios, cracking it against the table edge, and Seth turned back to his screen and started the query again from the top, just to watch nothing find itself.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1930s Dust Bowl followed the plowing of the Great Plains' native deep-rooted grasses, which had held the soil, so when drought came the wind carried the topsoil away.
story:
The gate to Mr. Novák's farm had a chain and a padlock, and Noah was the one with the key, which he turned every morning at six without thinking about it anymore. He had taken the job in April because he needed eleven hundred dollars by August, money his mother didn't have and wouldn't ask about, money that stood between him and the deposit at the state university. The work was simple and repetitive: checking fence, moving pipe, and, three times a week, hauling the mower along the field edges. Except the edges. Mr. Novák had drawn a map in April, a pencil line around every field, and inside that line nothing was to be cut.

Noah thought it was sentiment, some old man's fondness for weeds. The strips held thistle and foxtail and a scraggly native grass that Mr. Novák called by a name Noah forgot as soon as he heard it. A quarter of the acreage, doing nothing, in a year when the county had already gone eight weeks without rain.

The day the senior class came out on their environmental science trip, Noah was fixing the gate hinge, and Kyler and Miah found him there before the others got off the bus. Kyler had given the tour's opening speech at school, an elocution he'd rehearsed in the parking lot, all about stewardship, though Noah doubted Kyler had ever pulled a weed. Miah just asked whether they could get water. At the back of the barn, past the noxious-smelling tanks of fertilizer that made Noah's eyes sting even through the lid, there was a state historical marker Mr. Novák kept propped against the wall, brought from his grandfather's place in Kansas.

Kyler read it out loud, the way he read everything, as if for an audience. "The 1930s Dust Bowl followed the plowing of the Great Plains' native deep-rooted grasses, which had held the soil, so when drought came the wind carried the topsoil away." He looked up. "They had to put a marker up for dirt?"

"It's not for dirt," Miah said. She was squinting at the marker like it was a math problem. "It's for what happened when they took the roots out."

Noah had been about to say something about how that was Kansas, a hundred years ago, a long way from a farm with irrigation wells and no-till drills and a grain elevator visible from the road. But he thought of the strips. He thought of Mr. Novák standing at the field corner in May, saying only, "That's why the grass stays," and walking off before Noah could ask why. He had assumed it was about bees, or pheasants, something you could put on a brochure.

He didn't have to assume anymore, because three days after the class left, the wind came. It came out of the southwest at forty miles an hour and it did not smell like rain. Noah was in the equipment shed when the light outside turned the color of weak tea, and when he stepped to the door he could see the Anders field, the neighbor's quarter-section, tilled black to the fence line in June, lifting. Not the whole field, but the high spots, the places where the topsoil was thinnest, streaming off the surface in long brown ribbons that flattened against Novák's grass strips and stopped. By evening the strips looked like snow fences after a drift, piled on their windward side with soil that was not theirs. Novák's own fields, dried and cracked as they were, held.

They worked until dark, wetting down the yard so the dust wouldn't grind into the tractor's intake, and afterward Mr. Novák sat on the shed step with his coffee and let the wind burnish the rim of the cup to a dull shine where his thumb rested. He didn't give a speech. He said, "Anders will want a price on my seed mix now. He wouldn't take it free in March." That was all.

Noah did the arithmetic that night at his kitchen table, the way he did everything, with a pencil and two columns. Column one: eleven hundred dollars by August, deposit due the fifteenth, the mowing hours available if he took the strips too and sold the hay. Column two: a marker in a barn, and a fence line full of somebody else's topsoil. He understood, sitting there, that the two columns weren't really opposites, that the grass strips were economics as much as anything, insurance paid in land instead of money, and he also understood that he couldn't prove it. Maybe the wind would have spared Anders' field anyway. Maybe this year was an exception rather than a warning. He wrote both of those down too, because leaving them out felt like cheating.

He still didn't have a way to make both columns true at once. In the morning he drove out early, before the heat, and walked the west strip where the drift had piled highest, and found that under the caught soil the grass had gone to seed, thick seed heads he could strip off with his fingers and rub loose into a coffee can. It took him until noon to fill it. He was carrying the can up to the shed when Mr. Novák's truck came down the lane, and Noah heard himself say, before he had really decided anything, "Do you think I could stay on next summer? After my first year." Mr. Novák took the can from him, weighed it in one hand, and said, "You'll be the first one who ever asked to come back."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parallel parking, a driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first and then away as the car swings into the space.
story:
The laundromat occupied the corner of Marsh and Third, and behind it stretched a strip of cracked asphalt where the owner let Mr. Levy park his ancient Buick on Sundays, because Mr. Levy fixed the dryers for free and asked for nothing. Audrey had learned this the way she learned most things, by standing still and watching, and on the third Sunday of October she was standing in that lot with two milk crates and a folding chair, arranging them the width of a parking space apart.

"You're going to get us arrested," Casey said, dragging the second crate into position. She worked Saturdays at the laundromat counter and had the keys, which was how they had talked their way into the lot in the first place.

"Nobody gets arrested for parking," Audrey said. "That's the whole point of parking."

Her mother was at home sorting bills into piles, a penurious arithmetic Audrey could do in her sleep: the electric, the rent, the bus pass that had to last until the fifteenth. A license meant the job across town, the one that paid two dollars more an hour and required a car. A license meant a lot of things, and the test was in eleven days, and Audrey could not parallel park.

She had read the manual twice on the bus. She knew the rules the way she knew dates for history tests, cold and useless. When she backed the Buick toward the crates she ended up angled every time, rear wheels near the curb, front end swung out into the imaginary street like the car was trying to leave.

Mr. Levy came out around noon with a thermos of coffee and stood at the edge of the lot, saying nothing, which she had come to understand was his way of saying a great deal. He had taught his own daughter to drive in this same Buick, twenty years ago, in this same lot. Casey had told her that part.

On the ninth attempt Audrey sat with the engine idling, both hands on the wheel, and made herself stop repeating the manual and instead watch what her hands had been doing. She had been pulling in forward. That was the error, the whole error. You came in from alongside the car in front, and you reversed, and you turned the wheel toward the curb first, then away, as the car swung into the space. She said it out loud once, flat, the way you'd recite a phone number, and Casey laughed at her from the folding chair.

She pulled level with the crate that stood for the front car, checked her mirrors, and reversed, turning toward the curb until she felt the Buick's stern swing in, then turning away, and the car settled against the curb so gently that she had to look out the window to confirm she was inside the space. She got out and walked around the car twice, hands in her pockets, because if she touched anything she might break it. Casey took a picture of the crate-to-bumper gap with her phone. Mr. Levy poured a second cup of coffee and handed it over without comment.

The highway was harder, because the highway required faith in strangers. On the Thursday before the test Mr. Levy drove them out to the loop that ringed the city and made her merge into evening traffic, on-ramp shrinking under the tires, cars in the right lane deciding, one by one, whether she existed. The first time she slowed to a crawl and a truck had to swing around them, horn long and furious. The second time she held her speed and a gap opened where none had been, as if the traffic had fermented long enough and finally given way. Mr. Levy said only, "Again."

She was starting to understand that the test had nothing to do with fairness. It wasn't a meritocracy where studying hardest won; it was a matter of one examiner, one morning, one stranger's judgment of three seconds of her steering. She could do everything right and still fail on a bad gap or a hot temper in the passenger seat. That was the deal, and she had decided to take it anyway, the way you take most deals: with both eyes open and no guarantee.

Test day came cold and bright. The examiner was a woman with a clipboard and a cold, and she made Audrey park between two orange cones on a quiet street near the motor office. Audrey reversed in from alongside the front cone, turned toward the curb, then away, and felt the car swing true. She did not allow herself to smile until the woman said the word "pass," and even then the smiling felt borrowed, like the Buick, like the lot, like all of it.

She drove home with the paper license in her shirt pocket, past the laundromat with its windows steamed yellow, and saw Casey through the glass, arms full of towels, mouthing something she couldn't read. Audrey pulled to the curb, hazards blinking, and leaned across to open the passenger door. "Get in," she said. "We're going to the job place tonight, before I lose my nerve."

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: R. Edward Freeman's 1984 book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach argued that businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners.
story:
The pork chops had gone cold at Edouard's place, which his mother noticed before he did. He was pushing rice into a low ridge across one side of the plate, letting the grains undulate like a tiny landscape, and he did not stop until she said his name twice.

"Sorry. Long shift."

"You're allowed to eat while it's hot," his father said. "That's the whole point of a table."

Edouard cut into the chop and told them, because otherwise he would carry it upstairs whole. The district manager had come through the store on Tuesday, looked at the till receipts for twenty minutes, and by Wednesday night the new schedule was taped inside the break room. Closing shift now started at 5:30 instead of 4:00, which meant the store saved the overlap hour, two closers instead of three, and something about coverage during the rush. What it also meant was that Mara, who closed Tuesdays and Thursdays, would miss the 5:15 bus, the last one that connected to her street. The 6:40 existed on paper but arrived, in Mara's phrase, whenever it felt like it, and her mother didn't drive at night.

"So she quits?" his father asked, already reaching for the logic of it.

"She asked Mr. Dang if she could swap to mornings. He said mornings were full."

Mr. Dang was the front-end manager, the one who had hired Edouard in March and who kept a laminated photo of his own teenage self behind the register, presumably as a warning to others. He was not cruel. When a customer had screamed at Annabel over a coupon in April, he had stood beside her through the whole tirade and then bought her a drink from the cooler. But when Mara had asked about the swap, Edouard had been stocking the candy aisle close enough to hear the whole thing, and Mr. Dang had said the schedule was the schedule, that corporate did the math, and that she should think of it as the store doing what stores do. Then, softer, almost to himself: "Not everything that's good for the register is good for everybody standing near it."

Edouard had gone home that night and looked up whether anybody had ever formalized that feeling, because it seemed too large to be only his. It took him twenty minutes of bad search terms before he found it. In 1984, R. Edward Freeman published a book called Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach, arguing that businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners. Stakeholders. He read the word three times. Customers, workers, the neighborhood, all of it counted, all of it was the argument. He had wanted to run back to the store and hold the sentence up to the break room like a lamp.

At dinner his mother asked what he was smiling about, and he told them the fact the way he'd learned it, the year and the name and the title and the claim, and his father said, "They wrote a whole book about not being a jerk to your staff? Academics will study anything," which was facetious but not entirely wrong, and Edouard said the book was actually why he was having trouble eating. Because he had read further, past the part that felt like vindication, into the murkier part. If you counted everyone affected, you had to actually count them, weigh them, and the district manager would say he had: lower costs, lower prices, a store that stayed open, forty jobs preserved instead of trimmed. Who was Edouard to say Mara's bus outranked that? The trade-off didn't come with a scoreboard. The store hadn't intended to strand anybody. Nobody at corporate had ever heard of the 5:15. That was the part that sat worst in him, that harm could just happen, sideways, out of nobody's decision to be cruel.

"So what are you going to do," his mother said, not really asking, more tilting the evening toward it. "You can't fix a schedule."

"I traded shifts with her." He said it quickly, before it could sound like anything. "Tuesdays and Thursdays. I take close, she takes my Saturday mornings. I bike, so it doesn't matter when I get out."

His father said that was decent of him. His mother said it was more than decent. Edouard forked up the cold rice and thought neither word fit, exactly. It was something, and it was also a gesture the size of one bicycle, and tomorrow the schedule would still be taped to the wall, and Mr. Dang would still say the schedule was the schedule. He didn't know yet whether he'd say anything to Mr. Dang about the book, or whether quoting a 1984 business text at his manager over closing shifts would be brave or unbearable, probably both. Annabel had already texted him a photo of the 6:40 bus with the caption "ghost bus spotted, 23 minutes late, verisimilitude intact," and he'd laughed alone in the kitchen like an idiot.

After the plates were cleared he sat with his phone open to the passage about stakeholders, highlighting nothing, just reading it again. Then Mara's name lit the top of the screen. "You didn't have to do that," her message said, followed three seconds later by, "but I'm not giving it back."

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Risk compensation is the tendency of people to behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted.
story:
Madison would like it known that she saw the whole thing coming, that she had told Jay from the beginning exactly what would happen, though if you pressed her on the details she would admit, quietly, that she had mostly said "nice helmet" and nothing else. The helmet was genuinely nice, matte black with a chin strap that clicked like a seatbelt, and Jay had worn it to school on Tuesday even though he hadn't ridden his bike, just carried it through the halls like a trophy. Chantal had touched it and said it looked expensive. Jay said his dad had spent the money after the article, the one about how helmets prevent head injuries, and that he was now, quote, fully protected.

At lunch they sat on the low wall behind the portables, in that strange between-spaces strip of the schoolyard that Madison privately thought of as liminality made concrete, neither parking lot nor yard, fenced on three sides, good for nothing but sitting. Jay laid out his plan. There was a hill on Ridge Road, steep and straight, and he intended to take it faster than anyone in their grade ever had. He would be safe now, he said. That was the point of the helmet.

"Safe isn't a switch you flip," Madison said, and Jay asked her what she meant by that, and she found she didn't entirely know, so she said the hill was still the hill and he called her a grandma. Chantal laughed, and Madison laughed too, a little, because it was easier than holding her ground with nothing to stand on.

She remembered then, though she didn't say it, the autumn her mother had put antilock brakes on the old car and started following closer on the highway, drifting up the gap she used to keep, her hands looser on the wheel. Madison had watched this happen from the passenger seat for weeks, saying nothing, feeling clever and useless at the same time. She had a habit of noticing things and filing them away, which felt like a kind of responsibility but was really its opposite, a way of opting out while appearing engaged.

Thursday after last period, they all went to Ridge Road. Ms. Swampy, who lived in the blue house at the bottom of the hill and was rumoured to have once taught physics, was watering her mums, and she watched them gather with an expression Madison couldn't read. Jay clicked his chin strap. Twice, for emphasis. He said, "Full protection, full speed," and Madison thought of calling out something about the hill still being the hill, and didn't, and this is the part she can't suture shut no matter how she tells it afterward: the gap between what she noticed and what she did.

He came down fast, faster than Madison had ever seen anyone go on a bicycle, and the helmet did its job, which is to say his head was fine when he went over the gravel at the curve where the pavement went bad. His collarbone was not fine. His wrist was not fine. He lay in the ditch saying "I'm okay, I'm okay," while Chantal ran to Ms. Swampy's door and Madison stood there holding his bicycle, which had come out better than he had.

While they waited for the ambulance, Ms. Swampy brought a folded towel for his wrist and ice in a sandwich bag. She didn't lecture. She only said, nodding at the helmet, "I've seen that before. It's called risk compensation." Jay, grey-faced on the grass, said, "The what?" and Ms. Swampy said, "People feel protected, so they act less carefully, and the protection gives less than it should have." Then she went back inside, as if she had delivered a parcel and not a verdict.

On the walk home, Chantal kept saying the helmet had worked, technically, that his head was perfect, and Madison kept almost agreeing and then not agreeing, because it was a specious kind of comfort, true in its narrow way and false in every way that mattered: the helmet had been sold as protection, and it had become permission. Madison understood now that safety wasn't a property you could own, like a thing with a chin strap; it was a balance, a trade between what the gear gave and what the feeling of the gear took back, and Jay had spent the difference on speed. She understood, too, that she had watched the arithmetic happen and kept it to herself, which meant the hill was still the hill and the helmet was still the helmet and she was not quite the person she'd been telling herself she was.

She visited Jay on Saturday with a get-well card she'd spent too long choosing. His arm was in a sling and the helmet sat on his desk, scuffed at one temple, and he picked it up with his good hand and turned it over. "Still works," he said. "My dad says I could get back on the bike in six weeks." Madison looked at the helmet, then at him, then out the window at the street going downhill toward the corner, and said, "Six weeks is a long time to think about Ridge Road."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: An off-book rehearsal is one where actors must perform without their scripts, having memorised their lines.
story:
Nicole had taped a grid of the living room to the back of a cereal box, one square for every armchair and radiator, and she moved a bottle cap across it whenever an actor moved. Mr. Bélanger, whose drama club had lost its funding in the spring, had handed her the one-act before he left, along with three copies of the script and a piece of advice she still could not decide whether to trust. "A director decides," he had said. "That's the whole job." She was sixteen and had never decided anything larger than a seating chart, so she had set the schedule herself and printed it, and now it hung on the fridge with her mother's grocery list beneath it.

The living room smelled of dust and the pasta her mother had left warming on the stove. Alexi, who played the sister, knew every line cold and stood in the bay window mouthing them like a prayer. Samy sat on the couch with the script open on one knee, and every time Nicole looked over, the pages had turned backward, as if the play were being read in reverse.

"Thursday," Nicole said. "We agreed on Thursday."

Samy's face did something complicated. "Agreed is a strong word."

"It's the off-book date," Nicole said. "Off-book means no scripts. You perform the whole thing from memory." She heard her own voice flatten, the way her mother's did when reciting bus schedules, and she wondered whether authority was just boredom performed well.

"I know what it means." Samy turned a page. "I've been busy. My family's been a bit impecunious this month, I picked up shifts at the market, I'm tired when I get home." It was true; Nicole knew it was true, she had seen Samy's rusted bike chained outside the market at nine at night. And still the fact sat there unchanged: tomorrow the scripts went away, and Samy could not have recited the second scene if the stage were on fire.

Alexi came down from the window. "I could run lines with Samy tonight," she offered, in the tone of someone solving a math problem that was not hers.

"That's not the point," Nicole said, and then, because she did not know what the point was, she stopped.

She had spent the week trying to introspect, as her English teacher called it, about what kind of director she wanted to be, and the introspecting had produced two Nicole who argued in the shower. One believed that rules were the only kindness, that a deadline you moved for one person became a wall for everyone, that Alexi had memorised two hours of dialogue between shifts of her own. The other Nicole remembered Samy at thirteen, teaching her to juggle oranges in this same living room, patient through forty dropped fruit, saying "again" like it was a good word. That Nicole believed a director's real job was to see the actor under the role. Both Nicoles were plausible. Neither could prove the other wrong.

On the coffee table, half hidden under the drama folder, lay her chemistry homework, a diagram of ethene becoming polyethene, each small molecule labelled monomer, the chain it joined labelled something larger. She looked at it longer than the homework required. One unit, then another, then a thing that could hold weight. It was a coincidence of syllabus timing, and she knew it, and she let it mean something anyway.

"Okay," she said. "Here's what we do. Tonight Alexi runs lines with you, here, in this room, out loud. Tomorrow we go off-book on schedule. If you drop a line, you call it, and we take it again." She picked up the bottle cap and set it on the square marked couch. "And you start the play downstage left, not centre, because I want your first entrance to be a walk, not a stand."

Samy closed the script. "So I get tonight."

"You get tonight. Thursday is Thursday." She did not know if this was mercy or arithmetic, if she was seeing Samy or merely splitting the difference, and she suspected she would not know until the performance, or after, or never. Mr. Bélanger's three scripts sat stacked on the mantel, and tomorrow she would collect them all.

Alexi pulled a chair into the taped square marked window and said, "From the top, then. 'You came back for the photographs.'"

Samy stood, took a breath, and left the script face-down on the couch.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: If air resistance is ignored, a projectile's horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight, because no horizontal force acts on it.
story:
The garage smelled of chain oil and the ghost of a thousand sodas, and Nolan sat on an overturned milk crate with a whiteboard propped against Tucker's dad's lawnmower, trying to make a skateboard fly on paper.

"Again," Tucker said. He was lying on the hood of the car they weren't supposed to touch, tossing a tennis ball straight up and catching it, over and over, like a metronome for Nolan's suffering. "You got the skater going six meters last time. The ledge is only two meters off the ground, Nolan. He flew six meters and landed soft as a dove. That's not physics, that's a cartoon."

"He flew six meters because I made him fly six meters," Nolan said. "I wanted him to have a nice trip."

"He'd have a nice trip all right. Straight through the fence."

The problem had come from Mr. Teo, their neighbor, who had watched them at the skate park that afternoon and then ruined Nolan's whole evening by saying, in his mild way, that he could probably work out with a pencil and paper exactly where the skater would land. Mr. Teo taught at the college and kept a whiteboard in his garage, and he had written the ledge's height and the skater's speed at launch in blue marker and then gone inside to make tea, refusing to say anything more. "You know how to find how long things fall," was all he'd offered. "I've heard you argue about it."

Nolan knew how long things fell. Two meters took about two thirds of a second, something like that, and he could get it more precisely if he stopped doodling the skater as a stick figure wearing a tiny helmet. What he could not get was the other half. The skater left the ledge moving forward at some speed, and he fell, but he also traveled, and the two motions kept tangling in Nolan's head like headphones in a pocket. Every time he tried to combine them, he got a distance that changed its mind halfway through.

The tennis ball went up and came down. Up, down. Up, down.

"Stop doing that," Nolan said.

"It's helping you."

"It's mocking me."

Tucker's older brother's physics notebook sat open on the workbench, borrowed without permission, and Nolan had read the same page four times. He fell into a brief reverie about the notebook catching fire, which would be a shame, since the brother would kill them, but which would at least simplify things.

Then he noticed something he'd been skidding past. The page drew the flight as two separate arrows, and one of the arrows was labeled with the word constant. No horizontal force, the book said, so the sideways speed never changed from launch to landing. It didn't fade, didn't ease off, didn't get tired near the end. It just stayed what it was, the whole flight, like a friend who was boring but reliable.

Nolan sat very still, transfixed by how dumb the solution was. You didn't combine anything. You split it. The fall straight down took its own sweet time, and while it was taking that time, the forward motion just carried on at the same speed, unbothered, and the distance was the speed times the time and that was it. Two separate clocks, one skater.

"Wait," he said.

"No," said Tucker, who was phlegmatic about Nolan's eurekas, having survived several. "Absolutely not. Don't do the face."

"I'm doing the face."

He worked it fast. Two thirds of a second falling, more or less, and the skater left the ledge at maybe six meters a second, because Mr. Teo had clocked him on the flat with a phone app and had opinions about it. Six times two thirds. Four meters. He wrote 4 in the corner and boxed it, twice, in case it got away.

"Four meters," he announced. "That's where he lands. Four meters out from the ledge."

Tucker stopped throwing the ball. He was quiet in the way of someone doing the same math and arriving at the same number, which was the most convincing kind of quiet. "There's a bush at about four meters," he said finally. "The ugly one. He landed in it Tuesday."

"He landed in the bush."

"He landed in the bush."

They looked at each other. Somewhere inside the house a kettle began its thin complaint, and Mr. Teo came out with three mugs, setting one on the lawnmower beside the whiteboard. He looked at the boxed 4, at the two arrows, at Nolan, and raised his eyebrows a fraction, which from Mr. Teo was applause.

"Tomorrow," Tucker said, "we measure it. Tape measure, actual bush, and if it's four meters I will admit you're a genius. If it's five, you're a fraud and we tell everyone."

"It'll be close," Nolan said. Then, because honesty was cheaper before witnesses: "If it's not, I don't know which part I got wrong. The falling time or the speed at the ledge. They're not the same kind of wrong." He took the mug anyway.

"The skater's going to think we're insane," Tucker said, "measuring his bush."

"Come on," Nolan said, capping the marker. "Bring the tape measure."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
Reuben's kitchen smelled of burnt popcorn and printer ink, and the project was due in fourteen hours. Kelly-Anne had commandeered the good chair by the outlet, laptop balanced on her knees, scrolling through their slides one more time. Jason sat on the counter with the rubric in his hand, and that was where he saw it: slide six, the diagram of the immune response, with antigen and antibody labelled backwards.

"Slide six looks good," Kelly-Anne said.

Reuben looked up from cutting his sandwich into triangles. "Right? Took me an hour." He had drawn the diagram himself, and he had drawn it carefully, arrows in two colors, the invading particle in the middle wearing a little crown of proteins. He was proud of it in the quiet way he got proud, not bragging, just checking their faces to see if it landed.

The particle in the middle was labelled antigen, which was right, but so was the Y-shaped defender, which should have been the antibody, and Jason knew this because Mr. Korhonen had drilled it with a mnemonic two weeks ago that Jason had written on his hand before the quiz. He looked at Kelly-Anne. Kelly-Anne looked at the rubric in her own lap and did not look at the screen.

"Should we run it again from the top?" Reuben said.

It would take forty seconds to say the labels were switched. It would take nothing. But Reuben had spent an hour, and their grade was riding on the whole thing, and if Jason said it wrong, Reuben would do that thing where he went still and said "yeah, sure, whatever," and then the rest of the night would be a half inch of ice over all of them. Jason thought about the presentation in October, when Marcus had mispronounced a term through the whole rehearsal and nobody had said anything, and everyone had watched him say it wrong to the class anyway. Nobody had wanted to be the one. It had felt safer to let Marcus look foolish in public than to risk looking like a jerk in private.

Mr. Korhonen had a phrase for that, from some researcher, Amy Edmondson, 1999, psychological safety, a team's shared belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. Jason had written it down because it was going to be on the test, and now he was realizing it was not just on the test. Their team did not have it. Kelly-Anne had seen the diagram twice and said "looks good," which meant she was afraid of something, and it was not Reuben's sandwich knife.

"Hey, Reuben," Jason said, sliding off the counter. "Before we run it, I want to check one thing on six. The drawing's great, the arrows especially. But I think the labels got swapped. The crowned thing should be the antigen, and the Y-shaped one's the antibody." He kept his voice flat, the way you'd point out a page number. "It's a two-second fix because the drawing itself is right."

Reuben stared at the screen. Kelly-Anne went very still over her laptop. "I checked it," Reuben said.

"Which one's which?" Kelly-Anne said, and Jason winced for her, because that was not the way.

Reuben scrolled up to his notes. He scrolled back down. "The foreign particle," he said slowly. "Antigen. That's the mnemonic, the antigen is the intruder." He exhaled through his nose. "I swapped them. I was doing it at midnight." He highlighted, deleted, retyped. "Okay. Fixed." He looked at Jason for a second longer than was comfortable. "You could've just said it was wrong."

"It wasn't wrong. It was backwards in one place and right everywhere else," Jason said. "The drawing carried it."

Reuben turned back to the screen, but the ice had not formed. He cut one of his sandwich triangles in half and put the pieces on a napkin in front of Kelly-Anne and one in front of Jason, which was as close to thanks as he got. "Run it from the top," he said.

Kelly-Anne clicked to slide one. Somewhere upstairs a door slammed and Reuben's mother shouted down to ask if they wanted dinner, and Reuben shouted back "pizza," and started talking over the title slide with the diagram, correct now, glowing behind him.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.
story:
Robert had promised Mr. Becker he would explain DNA replication, transcription, and translation to the younger kids at the community garden by Saturday, and by Friday evening he still could not make the pieces fit together in his mouth. He sat on the back step with the textbook open on his knees, the pages soft from the humidity, and read the same paragraph four times. The paragraph said that before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together. He understood it the way he understood the bus route, which is to say he could recite it but could not drive it.

On Saturday morning he arrived early, before the little greenhouse had warmed, and found Jonas already there, unzipping his jacket by the pond because the sun had come out fierce. Jonas was garrulous by nature, a boy who could turn a five-minute errand into an hour's narration, but even he had failed the biology midterm, and so the two of them had been assigned to each other, the blind leading the blind.

"Look," Jonas said, holding the two halves of his unzipped jacket apart like wings. "My mom tried to explain it with this. The helicase is the zipper pull."

Robert watched the zipper teeth separate, one pair at a time, all the way down. "Except it's not teeth," he said slowly. "It says here it's the hydrogen bonds. The helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs, and that's what unwinds the double helix." He heard himself say it and, for the first time, believed it, because the jacket was right there opening in front of him and something in his chest opened with it. "Before anything else can happen, before the DNA can even be copied, it has to open. That's the first move."

The younger kids trickled in around ten, Scarlett among them, though she was Robert's age and had only come because her mother ran the garden and she had been promised she could leave early. She sat on an overturned bucket shelling peas and made no secret of listening.

Robert had brought supplies: pipe cleaners, paper tags for the bases, a hand-drawn diagram he was not entirely proud of. He handed the tags out and told the kids to pair up, A with T, C with G, and line themselves along a garden row like a strand. Then he walked to the middle of the row.

"I'm the helicase," he said, and he went down the line gently pulling the pairs of hands apart, one couple at a time. "The bonds holding you together, the hydrogen bonds, they break, and the helicase is what breaks them. That's how the double helix unwinds." The kids giggled as their hands came apart, and a small girl asked whether it hurt the DNA, and Robert said honestly that he did not think so, but that he did not know everything about it yet, which seemed to satisfy her more than a confident answer would have.

"Now each open side can be copied," he went on, walking the row again. "And later, a piece gets copied again, into a different kind of molecule, RNA, and that copy travels out to a place that reads it three letters at a time and builds a protein, one monomer after another, like threading beads." He held up a pea from Scarlett's bowl. "Like this. One bead, then the next, then the next. That's translation. The letters get transmuted into something that can actually do work in your body, an enzyme, a muscle fiber, whatever the body ordered."

"Where does the copy start, though?" Jonas asked, and Robert stopped, because that was exactly the part he had not mastered. He could describe the opening, the copying, the reading, but the timing, the signals, the regulation of it all, that territory was still dark to him.

"I don't know yet," Robert said. "I know the door opens first. I know how. I know the door is the enzyme called helicase and it breaks the hydrogen bonds holding the base pairs together, and the helix unwinds. After that I know the shape of the whole thing but not all the gears." He had learned, somewhere in the past month, that saying this plainly did not shrink him in anyone's eyes.

Scarlett had stopped shelling. She was looking down the row of kids with their pipe cleaners and paper tags, the paired letters, the empty space in the middle where Robert had walked.

"So the zipper opens," she said, "and then everything else in you gets built off the open halves."

"That's it," Robert said. "That's the whole semester in one garden row."

The small girl who had asked about pain was holding her A tag against a boy's T tag, pressing them together with both thumbs, testing the bond. Robert crouched beside her and did not stop her.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
story:
Tyson arrived at the community centre early enough to claim the good table, the one by the window where the afternoon light made the photocopied case packet legible. He spread the pages out and crossed his arms, an impermeable posture he had learned from his father, and read the hypothetical for the fourth time. A man at a rally, described in the fact pattern as an agitator, had stood on the steps of city hall and told a crowd that the council leader was a despot and that they ought to drag him out and burn his files. Someone had thrown a bottle. The state wanted him convicted of incitement.

"You're supposed to argue both sides," Eden said, dropping into the chair across from him. "That's the whole exercise. Ms. Fortin says the attorneys get twenty minutes for the state and twenty for the speaker."

"I know how it works."

"Then why do you look like the guy already confessed?"

Because the speech disgusted him, that was why, and because disgust made a poor opening statement. He said none of this. Eden slid a photocopy across the table, a page she had pulled from the library's constitutional law anthology. "Victor found this. He says it's the case the judges are going to want."

The page was Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969. Tyson read it twice, then a third time with his finger under the line. The Court had held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action. He copied the words onto a notecard, unhurried, because writing them by hand was how he kept things.

"So which side does it help?" Eden asked.

"Both," Tyson said. "That's the problem."

They spent the evening drilling. When he stood to argue for the state, Victor played the judges, slouched and merciless. Tyson laid out the crowd, the anger, the bottle already in the air. "The words were not philosophy," he said. "They were aimed at the people in front of him, and something happened within minutes." When he switched to the speaker's side, he had to dismantle everything he had just built, and the second argument came harder, because part of him wanted it to fail. "Imminent," he said. "Likely. The test doesn't exonerate my client's ideas. It doesn't say he's a good man. It says the state can punish this kind of talk only under these conditions, and the record doesn't show them." He believed it about half, which he suspected was how most advocacy worked.

Ms. Fortin convened the mock court on Saturday in the gymnasium, three folding tables draped with grey sheets for a bench, a badminton line taped over for the bar. Tyson argued first for the conviction, and he was good, he could feel it, the judges leaning in. Then he sat through a break, drank warm water from the fountain, and stood again as a different lawyer with the same mouth. Near the end a judge asked whether defending the man meant agreeing with him.

"No," Tyson said. "It means the test decides it, not me."

The judges conferred behind cupped hands. When the middle one, a college sophomore with a clipboard, announced that the speech was protected under Brandenburg, that it was not directed to inciting imminent lawless action and was not likely to produce such action, Tyson felt something loosening in his chest, pride or relief or the ugly small pleasure of being right.

Ms. Fortin gathered the sheets off the tables while the others stacked chairs. "You argued the second side better," she said. "The one you didn't believe on Tuesday."

"Tuesday was a different person."

"Maybe." She picked up his notecard from the counsel table, the one with the test copied out in his cramped hand, and held it out to him. "Next month is the appeal. Same case, new fact pattern. The speaker's lawyers are arguing that his later rally, the one with the torches, should be protected too, and you'll be facing them. You're counsel for the state this time." She waited while he took the card. "You've already written your opponent's best argument. Try to beat it."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Guessing a whole number from 1 to 100 by always picking the middle of the remaining range never takes more than seven guesses, which is binary search in game form.
story:
Maxime sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open to an empty file named search.py and forty-one hours until the assignment closed. The task from Ms. Foster was two parts: implement a search that found a number in a sorted list, and write a paragraph explaining why it beat checking every element from the front. He had read the specification three times. He had eaten two pieces of toast. He had not written a line of code.

Delaney had finished hers on Tuesday. "It's honestly short," she had said in the hallway, which was the kind of remark that helped nobody. Maxime's problem was not the typing. His problem was that he could not yet say, in his own sentence, why anyone would bother, and Ms. Foster graded the explanation as heavily as the program. He believed a thing he couldn't articulate about as far as he could throw it, which his grandfather had taught him was not far.

His grandfather had taught him something else first, the summer Maxime was eleven, on the screened porch where the old man did his crossword and refused air conditioning on principle. They had played a guessing game for coins. His grandfather would think of a whole number from 1 to 100, and Maxime got to ask higher or lower, and the winner kept the coin on the table between them. The first afternoon Maxime guessed 4, then 17, then 88, scattering himself across the range like a dropped box of matches, and lost four coins in a row. Then he noticed that his grandfather's first guess was always around the middle, never a corner, and he made himself do the same. After that his grandfather kept losing. Ten coins, then twenty, until the old man laughed, pushed the whole pile across, and said Maxime was the most perspicacious cheat he'd ever played. Maxime had not known the word. He'd looked it up inside, away from the mosquitoes, and decided it was the best thing anyone had ever called him.

He also, that summer, worked out the shape of it, though not the name.
