Whatever the number was, if he always picked the middle of what remained, the possibilities fell into halves, and halving a hundred ran out fast. He remembered counting it on his fingers: never more than seven guesses, ever, from 1 to 100. Seven, and then the game was over and the coin was his. He had no idea this had anything to do with computers, because he was eleven and computers were for a game about zombies.

At the kitchen table, nine hours into his deadline and fighting off the somnolence that came from reading documentation after dinner, he opened the assignment page again and stopped at a sentence he had skimmed past. The strategy you used in a number-guessing game has a name, it said, and the name was binary search. He read it twice. Something from the porch and something from the classroom, two rooms he had always kept separate, turned out to open onto each other, and he had been compartmentalizing them for six years without knowing. He got himself a glass of water and came back and started typing.

The doorbell rang at nine. It was Delaney, holding her own laptop and a bag of chips, saying her wifi was out and her mother's house was unbearable and could she work at his table. He moved his charger over. She sat down across from him, the way she had since they were assigned adjacent seats in grade nine, and watched his screen while pretending not to.

What Delaney saw, over the top of her laptop, was Maxime writing a loop. She was not nosy by nature, but she had spent two days on this same assignment and she recognized the shape of it, the way a runner recognizes another runner's gait. He was taking a list, sorting it because the specification said to assume sorted data, and cutting the range in half each time by comparing the middle. She had done the same thing and understood it only as a procedure, a recipe she'd copied from a diagram and gotten working on the third try. She had never once connected it to anything outside the editor. Watching him, she noticed he kept pausing with a small private half-smile, like someone hearing a joke the rest of the room hadn't caught. She wondered what the joke was.

"You're smiling at your code," she said. "That's concerning."

"Play a game with me," Maxime said. He pushed his laptop aside. "Think of a whole number, one to a hundred. Don't tell me. I get yes-or-no higher-or-lower."

"You're avoiding the assignment."

"This is the assignment. Think of a number."

She thought of 83, made her face blank, and said go. He said fifty. Higher. Seventy-five. Higher. Eighty-seven. Lower. Eighty-one. Higher. Eighty-four. Lower. Eighty-two. Higher. Eighty-three. She stared at him. "That's creepy. Do it again." He did it again with 9, and it took five guesses, and with 100, which took seven, and she pushed the chips to the middle of the table the way his grandfather used to push coins.

"It never takes more than seven," Maxime said. "Any number, one to a hundred, if I always guess the middle of what's left. Seven, worst case." He pulled the laptop back and turned the screen so she could see the loop, the low and the high, the middle recalculated after every answer. "That's what I'm implementing. It's called binary search. My grandfather taught me the game before I knew the word. Now I have both halves."

Delaney looked at her own screen, at her working, copied recipe, and did not say anything for a moment. "So the paragraph," she said slowly. "If the list has a million sorted things, and yours keeps halving instead of marching from the front."

"Yeah."

She began deleting her paragraph. Maxime watched her cursor eat four sentences and kept his mouth shut about the two hours she'd spent on them. "I still don't get why it works," she said. "Not fully. I can do it and I can't quite say it."

"Same," Maxime said. "I can say it never takes more than seven from one to a hundred because I counted it on a porch when I was eleven. Why the halving is that powerful, mathematically, I'd be making it up." He typed a comment at the top of his file: check the why later, before the deadline. Then he ran the program, and the found it printed on the screen, in position six.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958; the resulting graph is called the Keeling Curve.
story:
The printer in the library had been jammed since third period, which Chloe took personally, because the presentation was due at nine the next morning and her slides currently existed only on a laptop with a battery that held a charge the way a sieve held water. She had chosen the carbon dioxide graph on purpose, back when the assignment felt abstract: the one that climbed in a slow, sawtooth line from the left edge of the frame to the right, like a staircase built by someone who kept changing their mind and then not changing it at all. Now the graph was her responsibility, and she could not remember where it came from.

"You could just say Hawaii," Charlize said, sitting across the table with her own project spread out, a poster about ocean plastics that she was decorating with a cartoon turtle. "Nobody's going to fact-check Hawaii."

"Somebody might. Ms. Nielsen fact-checks everything." Chloe scrolled through a search page so dense with results that the actual answer seemed to be hiding in it deliberately. She knew the measurements were old, older than her parents. She knew they were taken somewhere high, on a volcano, because the air up there was supposed to be clean of local pollution. She could picture the station, white buildings against dark rock, and she could not for the life of her name it.

Charlize offered the turtle poster for moral support and then, when that was declined, a piece of gum. What she did not offer was mercy. "You have five tabs open about the ocean. Do you even know what Scripps is?"

"It's an institution. Of oceanography." Chloe said it with the flat confidence of someone reading the words off a tab title, which she was. She clicked through, and the name arrived all at once, unremarkable and complete: a man, Charles David Keeling, who had begun regular measurements of carbon dioxide in March 1958. Regular meant every interval, no gaps, decade after decade, the kind of patience that seemed almost pathological until you saw the line it produced.

"So it's a person," Charlize said, leaning over to look. "A guy measured air and now there's a graph."

"There's more than a graph." Chloe followed a link and landed on the station itself, perched on Mauna Loa, and the sawtooth pattern she'd been squinting at for a week suddenly had a geography and a start date and a name attached to it. "They call it the Keeling Curve," she said, mostly to the screen.

"That's the least surprising name in science," Charlize said. "Man measures thing, thing named after man. The turtle doesn't even get that."

The next morning Ms. Nielsen stood by the window while Chloe presented, arms folded, radiating the specific attention of a teacher who has already decided to ask one question and is only waiting to see if you will preempt it. Chloe explained the greenhouse effect first, because she had learned the hard way in rehearsal that jumping straight to the graph left everyone behind: sunlight came through, the earth warmed, certain gases in the atmosphere absorbed the heat radiating back out and returned it, the way a blanket returns your own body heat to you, except the blanket kept getting thicker. She made herself say "infrared radiation" twice so it would stop sounding foreign in her mouth. Then she put the graph on the projector and gave the facts she had hunted down, in order, the way she'd found them: Scripps Institution of Oceanography, a man named Keeling, regular measurements beginning in March 1958, on Mauna Loa in Hawaii, and the line they produced, climbing, with small annual dips like breath being drawn.

She paused on the word "breath" because she had not planned it and it had arrived anyway.

Ms. Nielsen's question, when it finally came, was not the one Chloe had braced for. "Why do you believe this graph?" she asked. "You didn't collect the data."

Chloe stood there for a moment. The honest answer assembled itself slowly: she believed it because the measurements had been taken the same way, in the same place, by an unbroken method, for longer than her whole life, and because the people who continued them had no obvious reason to invent a staircase. But she also knew that she was eighteen and had personally verified nothing, that belief here was a kind of trust, and she said so. "I can't check it myself. I can only check that a lot of independent people tried to and failed to break it."

Ms. Nielsen nodded once, which was the closest thing to clemency she issued during presentations, and called on Ashlynn, who had spent the period looking progressively more bellicose about being next.

Afterward, packing up, Chloe found a sticky note on her laptop in Charlize's handwriting: "the turtle has no name. think about it." She was still smiling at it when she got to the parking lot and discovered that her car, which she had left charging overnight at the one working outlet, had drawn exactly four kilometres of range, because the school had shut the exterior power off at six. She looked at the graph of her own prospects, then down the hill toward town, and started walking.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: In 1936 the Literary Digest poll collected about 2.4 million responses yet predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt, who then won in a landslide.
story:
The argument started before the bell finished ringing, the way arguments in fourth period always did, with Chace holding his phone above his head like a verdict. He had found a poll online, forty thousand respondents, showing the school board's levy would fail by eleven points, and he was waving the number at anyone who would look. "Forty thousand people," he said. "You can't argue with forty thousand people."

Anthony slid into his seat and pulled his notebook out without looking at it. He had been the one who started this, indirectly, by telling Chace last week that the levy mattered, that the band program and the intramural leagues and half the things Tyrell cared about would go first if it failed. Tyrell sat in front of him now, turned around, arms folded on the back of the chair, watching Chace the way he watched a defender before a cut.

"Where'd they get the forty thousand?" Anthony asked.

"It's on the internet," Chace said. "There's a link."

"That's not where they got the people. That's where they put the result." Anthony leaned forward. "Think about who ends up on a site like that. Who has the time, who's already mad enough to click through the whole thing."

Chace scrolled, then turned the screen as if it settled the matter. "It's the biggest poll anyone's run. Bigger than anything on TV."

That was the sentence that sent Anthony backward in his mind, into his grandfather's bookshelf and the afternoon last summer he'd spent avoiding packing for college by reading whatever was on it. One of the books had a chapter on the 1936 election, and he had read it twice because he hadn't believed it the first time. He said it now carefully, the way you carry water in your hands. "In 1936, the Literary Digest ran a poll. They got about 2.4 million responses. Two point four million. And they predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt." He paused. "Roosevelt won in a landslide."

Ms. Moose, who had been writing the day's problem on the board, set the marker down and turned around, but she didn't say anything. She had this way of going still when a conversation caught fire, as if she were grading it in her head.

"Two point four million," Chace repeated.

"And they got it wrong anyway." Anthony spread his hands. "So it can't just be about how many."

The room went quiet in the way it did when someone had knocked a pillar loose. Then Tyrell said, "Then what's the point of any of it? My mom keeps asking me if the levy's going to pass, because if it doesn't, they're cutting the free lunch program at my little brother's school, and I keep telling her I don't know. Nobody knows."

Ms. Moose walked the problem to the board and stood beside it. The problem was about a confidence interval, a phrase Anthony had seen in the textbook but hadn't touched until now. She read it aloud once, then said, "Work it in pairs. When you disagree, that's the assignment." And she sat down at her desk, which was how she ended every lesson she actually cared about.

Anthony and Chace pulled their chairs together, and Tyrell swung around to make it three. The numbers came slowly. There was a percentage, a sample size, a range that the true value could fall inside, and Anthony found himself staring at the width of that range, which was wider than the gap in Chace's poll. He said so before he could stop himself. "The margin's bigger than their lead. Forty thousand people, and the spread is still wider than eleven points."

"So the poll doesn't say it fails," Tyrell said slowly. "It says nobody knows."

"It says something tighter than that," Anthony said, and then realized he didn't know what it said, not exactly, and said that too. "There's a real difference between a poll being wrong and a poll being quiet. The Digest wasn't quiet. It was wrong, loudly, with two point four million people behind it. This one might just be quiet." He tapped the textbook. "I can't tell which yet."

Chace had gone back to his phone, but not to argue. He was looking for the poll's method page, and when he found it, buried three links deep, he read it aloud in pieces. Respondents recruited through a fan site for local politics. Anyone could forward it. No weighting. He looked up. "So the people who answered were the people who already talk about this stuff."

"Happenstance," Anthony said. "The whole sample is happenstance stacked on happenstance. It looks like a fortress and it's built out of whatever drifted by."

Tyrell was writing something in his own notebook, not the math. Anthony glanced over and saw a list: addresses, a time, Saturday. "What's that?"

"If nobody knows," Tyrell said, "then nobody's decided. I'm making a flyer for Saturday. My brother's school, the rec league, the church on Fillmore. Ten minutes each, then I'll say we have thirty people and a margin of error of about a hundred percent, and we'll knock on doors anyway." He tore the page in half and offered one side to Chace. "You're good at links. Make one people can actually find."

Chace took the paper, and after a second he put his phone face down on the desk, which for him was practically a signature. Ms. Moose looked up from her grading, and Anthony could not read whether she was pleased or only patient, but she wrote something small in her book.

At the door after the bell, Tyrell stopped him. "Saturday, nine o'clock. You in?"

Anthony thought about the subterranean hum of the empty band room, the instruments nobody would fund, the range on the board wider than anybody's certainty. "I'm in," he said. "Bring the flyers."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
Austin had promised himself he would finish the chapter before Keven arrived, but the paragraph kept sliding out of focus. He was reading the scene where Mr. Bennet tells Elizabeth she must marry Mr. Collins, and though he could follow every sentence, he could not say why Ms. De Vries had flagged it for their seminar. The assignment was to apply a critical lens, feminist or Marxist, and Austin had chosen Marxist mostly because Keven had, and Keven had chosen it because it sounded like less reading.

The library was nearly empty at four o'clock on a Tuesday. He had spread his books across the table by the window, taking up more room than he needed, and when Cecilia set her bag down across from him she moved two of them without asking. She had the same novel open, a different edition, its margins already crowded with ink.

"You picked the feminist one?" he asked, nodding at her page.

"I picked the scene where he laughs at her," Cecilia said. "He's known Mr. Collins is ridiculous for twenty years and he lets his daughters find out on their own, one proposal at a time. He owns the house. If he dies, it goes to Collins. That's the whole joke." She tapped the margin. "I kept wondering why she has to be the clever one and still be stuck."

Keven dropped into the third chair with a bag of vending machine chips and said, "It's obviously Marxist. The entail, the inheritance, the whole economy of who marries whom. Marriage is the market. Austen basically says it."

"Basically," Cecilia said, in the tone she used when she thought someone was being confident about something half-understood.

Austin looked back at the page. The entail was a fact, sure, a legal mechanism, but Ms. De Vries had warned them in class that a lens was not the same as a topic. Any stratum of the novel could be the topic; the lens was what you looked through. He tried it, holding the marriage plot up as a transaction, and something did shift: Elizabeth's refusal of Collins stopped looking like wit and started looking like a worker declining to sell the only thing she has. But the reading felt reductive in a way he couldn't name, as if it flattened the parts he actually liked, the irony, the voice.

He said so, and Keven shrugged. "That's the point. It strips the varnish off."

"Or it strips off the wrong layer," Cecilia said. "The varnish is the thing. She wrote the jokes."

Austin went to find Ms. De Vries, who was shelving returns in the 800s with the unhurried precision of someone who knew every book's place. He asked her, without quite planning to, why so few of the novels on their reading list had been written by women. It had been bothering him since Cecilia counted them on her fingers last week and ran out of fingers.

Ms. De Vries didn't answer directly. She pulled a slim book from the cart instead and set it in his hands. "Woolf," she said. "A Room of One's Own, published in 1929. She argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction." Then she went back to shelving, as if she had merely handed him the right call number.

He carried it to the table and read standing up. Woolf's reasoning was not about talent or permission but about conditions, about who could afford the time and the quiet. Austin had never thought of a room as something that had to be bought. His own room was down the hall from his sister's, and the door closed, and nobody had ever told him it was unusual. He thought of Elizabeth Bennet again, clever in a house she could not keep, and the Marxist reading and Cecilia's reading stopped seeming like rivals. The entail was the machinery; Woolf was asking why so few women ever got to build anything with the machinery at all. Together they made a shape he hadn't seen from either alone.

"That's the one," Cecilia said, looking over his shoulder. "I kept checking it out and returning it unread."

Austin sat down and wrote at the top of his notes a question instead of a thesis: what does the novel look like if we read Elizabeth's wit as unpaid labor? It was, he admitted to them, not exactly an answer. Maybe wit was resistance and maybe it was entertainment and maybe Austen would have laughed at both claims. Keven read it over and frowned, then conceded, grudgingly, that the class thing and the woman thing might be "the same pressure from two directions," which was as close to changing his mind as Keven ever got in public.

At closing time they gathered their books, and Cecilia paused at the front desk to check out the Woolf for herself. The librarian stamped it, and outside the window the streetlights had come on all down the block, each one marking a room where someone, tonight, was reading or not reading, writing or not writing. "Five hundred a year," Cecilia said, reading the last page as they walked out. "She thought even that was enough." Austin held the door and wondered what his room would cost, and whose.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
Henry arrived at the coffee shop eleven minutes early, which he told himself was a coincidence of bus schedules and not evidence that he cared. He chose a table near the window and arranged his phone face down, the way a person with nothing to hide would. Aria was ten minutes late, which was fine, and when she swept in she kissed his cheek before he'd stood up, which was also fine, and when she pulled out his chair for him by gripping his shoulder to steer him into it, that was fine too. He was sixteen and this was a first date and the whole point of a first date was to be gracious about things.

She ordered for both of them without asking, a gesture he decided to find decisive rather than strange, and while they waited she told a story about a teacher she'd eviscerated in front of the whole class, in exact and merciless detail, and Henry laughed in the right places. When he reached for his cup and she caught his wrist and held it to keep his hand still while she finished a point, he noticed that his knuckles had gone white under her fingers. He decided this was a sign of animation. Some people were simply emphatic.

Rihanna appeared at the counter with Mathias, both of them clutching biology flashcards, and Henry understood immediately that this was not an accident. Rihanna had been the one, three days ago at lunch, who had watched Aria grab Henry's arm in the hallway hard enough to leave marks and had gone quiet in that specific way of hers. He had told her it was nothing, that Aria was intense, that some people expressed themselves physically. He had almost believed it. Now Rihanna ordered a hot chocolate and drifted over, casual as weather.

"You two look cozy," she said, and then, to Aria, "You're in my econ class. You argued about marginal cost for twenty minutes."

"I stand by it," Aria said, smiling, and her hand settled onto the back of Henry's neck.

Mathias hovered, shuffling his cards. Rihanna didn't leave. She talked to Aria about the econ teacher, about a track meet, and the whole time Henry could feel her watching the hand, watching the way Aria's thumb pressed small controlled circles into his skin. When Aria went to the counter for a napkin, Rihanna leaned in fast.

"I looked it up last night," she said. "The CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey. About one in twelve US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence. That's students who dated. Reported it."

"I know what a survey is," Henry said.

"One in twelve, Henry."

"You're being dramatic." His voice came out flatter than he intended. "She's just enthusiastic. You don't know her."

"I know what I saw in the hallway. That wasn't enthusiasm. That was her making sure you couldn't leave."

He wanted to argue and found he couldn't locate the argument. His mind felt like a steppe, wide and level and bare, one thought visible all the way to the horizon: that he had been narrating the evening to himself in a voice that kept smoothing things over. He had been an unreliable witness to his own arm.

Aria came back with the napkin and, in a gesture that felt sudden and gratuitous, swept the napkin across the table so that his cup tipped and coffee spread toward his sleeve. "Oops," she said, bright, and took his hand to inspect the stain, squeezing his fingers together until they ached, her smile going out to Rihanna like a flag planted in the last unclaimed ground.

"Let go of his hand," Rihanna said.

"Excuse me?"

"You heard me."

Aria released him, slowly, keeping eye contact, and Henry sat there with his damp sleeve and his aching fingers and the strange relief of a thing finally being said out loud, of a fact standing in the middle of the table where no one could narrate it away. He didn't know yet what he'd do, whether he'd stand up or stay, whether one in twelve was a number about him or about other people, whether you could like someone and be afraid of them in the same minute. He picked up his cup, set it upright, and looked at Aria.

"I need to think," he said. "I'm going to walk home."

"Sit down, Henry," Aria said.

He stood up.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The top of most population pyramids has more women than men, because women live longer than men on average.
story:
Olivier had taped the population pyramid of Japan into the back of his notebook, and on Saturday he brought the notebook up the trail, because Mr. Saleh had assigned each of them a country and a question: does this place need more schools or more nursing homes, and how can you tell? The trail climbed through pine shade above the town, and Bella walked ahead of him with Skyler, both of them arguing about whether the swim coach was a charlatan for charging forty dollars to analyze a stroke he had never coached anyone to fix. Olivier lagged, holding the notebook open against his thigh, turning the pyramid sideways every few steps as if a different angle might make it speak.

"It's shaped like a Christmas tree," Skyler said, dropping back to look. "Young people at the bottom, old people at the top. Is that good or bad?"

"Depends what you're planning," Olivier said. He stopped at a switchback where the view opened, the whole valley brassy with September light. "Mr. Saleh says the bars are ages. Bottom is zero to four, all the way up to the over-eighties. If it's wide at the bottom, there are lots of kids. You'd build schools. If it's wide up here," he tapped the top of the page, "you'd build nursing homes."

Bella came back down to them, took the notebook, and frowned at it for a long moment. "Why is the right side fatter at the top? Look. All through the top, the right-hand bars stick out past the left ones. Is that a typo?"

They bent over it together, three heads over one page, while a jogger picked her way past on the outside edge of the switchback. Skyler guessed first. "Maybe they count women twice? Like, some mistake in the census?" Bella guessed second. "Maybe more girl babies in Japan?" But the asymmetry didn't run down the whole pyramid, only the top, and Bella, tracing the bars with her finger, realized the gap widened the older the age group got. "It's not at birth," she said slowly. "It grows. So it's something about getting old."

Olivier sat down on a flat rock with the notebook and thought about his grandmother, who had outlived his grandfather by nine years and kept his jacket hanging by the door. He thought about the widows on his own street, four of them on one block, and how he had never once asked himself why that pattern existed. He had wanted the pyramid to be a machine you could read mechanically, wide bars meaning cradles or beds, but here was a wrinkle the machine hadn't accounted for. The top of the pyramid had more women than men, because women lived longer than men on average. He said it out loud, experimentally, testing it against the page. The bars agreed with him everywhere.

"So the country needs more nursing homes," Skyler said, "and most of the people in them will be women. That's strange. That's like, all these old women, and all these old men who aren't there."

"Would knowing that change what you build?" Bella asked. Olivier liked that she asked questions like that, questions with no obvious floor beneath them. He tried to historicize the pyramid, to ask what forces had stacked it into this shape and what era it belonged to, but the more he pushed, the more it slipped out from under him. He could describe the pattern. He could not say where it was going.

"Here's what I keep running into," he said as they started up again, the switchbacks tightening toward the ridge. "For the assignment I can say schools or nursing homes and be done. But the pyramid is one year, a snapshot. It can't tell me what it looked like thirty years ago or what it'll look like in thirty. Mr. Saleh wants a prediction, and a snapshot isn't a prediction, it's just a photograph of people who are already alive." He wasn't sure that distinction was as clever as it felt, and he said so, and Bella said that admitting it was probably worth more marks than faking certainty, though Mr. Saleh might disagree.

"He told us the reward for the assignment is extrinsic," Skyler said. "His word. Grades. He said if we found it interesting, that part was on us."

"I did find it interesting," Olivier said, surprised at himself. "I found it interesting before it was going to get me anything." That, too, he couldn't entirely explain, the way a fact could sit inert in a textbook for a week and then, on a rock above a valley, suddenly seem to want something from him: a decision, a next question, a reason the right side of the top outlived the left.

At the ridge they stopped to drink water and look back at the town, small and exact below them, its school roofs visible among the trees. Bella folded the notebook and handed it to him. "So write it with the wrinkle in," she said. "Nursing homes, and most of them full of women, and say what you don't know. He asked us to read the pyramid, not to be its charlatan." Olivier slid the notebook into his pack, and the three of them stood a moment longer at the top, where the trail went on without them, narrowing north into the trees.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In plant and animal cells, introns are cut out of newly made RNA and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
story:
The trail behind the school cut through a strip of woods that nobody seemed to own, and Leo walked it every evening that week with his biology textbook under his arm like a hostage. On Monday he had stood in front of Mr. Sadeghi's class and explained how DNA is copied and turned into protein, and the explanation had collapsed somewhere between transcription and translation, two words that had looked so distinct on the flashcards and so identical in his mouth. Mr. Sadeghi had given him until Friday to say it again, aloud, one on one. Leo's father called it a second chance. Leo called it arbitration, a ruling on whether he deserved to graduate with the rest of them.

Alexis was already at the creek bend when he arrived on Wednesday, tripod legs splayed in the mud, filming a video for her own application portfolio. She was narrating to the camera about the woods, flubbing the third sentence, stopping, starting over. Leo sat on the flat rock they had claimed since tenth grade and watched her do it eleven times.

"You're wasting the memory card," he said.

"I'm not wasting anything. I cut the bad takes out tonight and splice the good ones together. That's the whole job." She checked the frame, unsatisfied, moved the tripod half a metre upstream. "Why are you carrying that book like it bit you?"

He told her about Friday. He told her that he could recite the steps and still not narrate them, that when he tried to say how the DNA was copied into RNA and how the RNA was then read off to build a protein, the sentences slid into each other like wet paint. Alexis listened the way she listened to everything, with her whole face turned toward him, which was flattering and also made his heart palpitate in a way he declined to examine.

"Do it for the camera," she said.

"Nobody wants a video of me failing biology."

"Nobody will ever see it. I'll delete it after. Come on, you explain better when you're pretending to be someone who explains well." She had aimed the lens at the rock before he agreed, which was her way of removing the arbitration from his hands entirely.

So he talked to the camera, and failed, and talked again, and Alexis called out "bad take" each time with the bored cruelty of a director. On the ninth or tenth attempt he was in the middle of describing the newly made RNA when she interrupted him. "Wait, wait. Is that the part where it gets edited?" He said he didn't know what she meant. She said, "Like my video. Before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus, in plant and animal cells, the introns get cut out of the newly made RNA and the exons that are left get spliced together." She said she had done a report on it in the fall, had liked the sound of the words, introns and exons, the thrown-away parts and the kept parts. Leo stared at her. The textbook had said this and he had read past it, because it had looked like a detail, when it was actually the shape of the whole thing: a copy that gets cut and joined before it travels, a message assembled out of what survives the editing.

He made her run the take again. He said it all, the copying, the cutting, the spliced message leaving the nucleus, the reading of it into protein, and for the first time it held together, because he was no longer reciting steps but telling one story about a transcript being trimmed. He wanted to kiss her or thank her and did neither, because Jesse arrived then down the trail with two slushies, the third member of their old trio, back for a week before his family moved for good, and the evening broke into easier talk.

Thursday night Alexis texted that she had not deleted the footage. She had cut it together, spliced out the bad takes, kept the ninth one and the last one, and sent it to Mr. Sadeghi, because Mr. Sadeghi was her uncle, a fact Leo had somehow never absorbed, and she thought a man who assigned an oral retake might prefer to hear it early. Leo sat on his bed with his heart going wrong again, furious and grateful in the same breath, unable to tell which one was winning, and typed and deleted three replies, each one an exon, each one cut.

On the trail Friday he found Mr. Sadeghi waiting on the flat rock, phone in hand, the video apparently watched. "Say it once more," Mr. Sadeghi said, "to me, this time." Leo put down the textbook, and began.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
Sofia got the interview because her mother knew Mr. Buchanan's wife from the clinic, and she got the job because she showed up ten minutes early and said yes to Saturday mornings. The store was called Buchanan's Hardware and Deli, which sounded like a mistake until you walked in. Power tools and paint occupied the front half, and in the back, behind a swinging door, there was a meat counter with a slicer, a case of cold cuts, and a rack of chip bags that no one had dusted in a while. Small towns made room for these arrangements.

Her mother had made her read the state's youth employment page before the interview, the way some mothers made their daughters carry pepper spray. Sofia had scrolled past it on her phone on the drive over, mostly out of politeness, and one line had caught her because it was stranger than the rest. Workers under eighteen, it said, may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant. She had read it twice. It seemed oddly specific, like a rule written after something happened somewhere, and she had thought about it that night with a small feeling of foreboding she couldn't justify, lying in bed listening to the furnace.

On her second Saturday she restocked bolts and learned the register from Kayleigh, who had worked there since the spring and who explained that the trick was never to malign the gas station across the road, because half the customers had relatives who owned it. Kayleigh was seventeen and saving for a car that she described, without embarrassment, as phenotypically identical to a piece of rust. She had a biology test Monday and recited vocabulary between customers, tapping the counter in rhythm. Dominant, recessive, phenotypic, genotype.

At eleven, Mr. Buchanan came through the swinging door wiping his hands. "Morgan called in. Sofia, can you cover the deli for an hour? Just slicing the lunch orders, it's nothing."

Sofia stood very still behind the register. "I'm sixteen."

"So?"

She hadn't planned to say anything. The rule had sat in her phone for two weeks like a stone in a pocket, and now it was in her mouth. "Federal rules. Anyone under eighteen can't operate a power-driven meat slicer. Not even in a grocery store deli or a restaurant." She heard how it came out, flat, like the webpage itself, and regretted the flatness but not the content.

Mr. Buchanan looked at her for a long moment. He was not a man who raised his voice; he was a man who set down his rag. "Where'd you hear that?"

"My mom made me look up the rules before I started. I don't know why it stuck."

He pulled out his own phone and typed with one finger for a while. Kayleigh pretended to alphabetize the sandpaper. Then he put the phone away and pushed through the swinging door, and through it Sofia heard him on the landline, asking Rosa from the bakery counter if she could come in for an hour. When he came back out he said, "You'll do stock and register only," and nothing else, and the matter seemed closed except that it wasn't, because it never is when a rule collides with a schedule.

The lunch rush came and went. Rosa, who was sixty and fast, sliced turkey and told a story about her brother's fence. Sofia rung up drill bits and tried to decide what she felt. She had not lied, and she had not done anything wrong, and yet Morgan would lose an hour of pay because Morgan was also sixteen and had said yes without knowing, and Mr. Buchanan would now look at Sofia differently, though whether with respect or irritation she couldn't tell. Kayleigh leaned on the counter beside her during a slow stretch.

"You did the right thing," Kayleigh said. "Also Rosa has been trying to get more hours for a month, so."

"Both can be true," Sofia said.

"That's very phenotypic of you," Kayleigh said, and laughed at her own joke, and Sofia laughed too, and then a customer came in wanting roofing nails, and she went to find them.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
The envelope from Sal's Diner was thin, and Dylan had already spent the money in his head three different ways before he opened it: gas, a decent pair of shoes, a month of not asking his mom for twenties. The number inside was smaller than any of those plans. He counted the digits twice, then a third time, as if the ink might rearrange itself out of pity.

He'd worked thirty-one hours at eleven dollars an hour. That math was not hard. He did it on the back of a placemat from the diner's takeout stack, the kind with a cartoon milkshake extruding a straw at a cheerful angle, and got three hundred forty-one dollars. The check said two hundred ninety-two and change. Somewhere between his hours and the paper, forty-nine dollars had walked out the door, and he wanted its forwarding address.

Israel was refilling the ketchup bottles when Dylan held up the placemat math. "Read this and tell me where I got robbed."

Israel squinted. "You didn't. That's Social Security. They take six point two percent of your wages off every check. It's right there on the stub, see, FICA. Everybody thinks their first check is a mistake. Mine, I thought the diner was punishing me personally."

"Six point two percent," Dylan repeated, doing it out loud. "That's like twenty-one bucks." He looked at the stub again. There it was, one line among lines, quiet as a fingerprint. "And that just happens forever?"

"Until you make a pile of money, my dad says. There's a limit on it for the year, some high number of wages. After your wages pass that, they stop taking it. He says rich guys in December get checks with no Social Security taken out at all, and he says it in a voice like he's describing a crime scene."

Nevaeh slid into the booth across from Dylan with her own check in hand, since it was Friday and Ms. Hamdan paid everyone the same afternoon, in person, with a little nod that made it feel like a ceremony. "Are we doing the betrayed-by-your-paycheck thing? Good, I have opinions." She flattened her stub on the table. "I did this in October. I cried in the walk-in freezer, which is disgusting and I don't recommend it, but then I did the math and got over it. Sort of. Sixty percent over it."

"It's not even that much money," Dylan said, surprising himself by defending the missing twenty-one dollars. "It's the principle of it. I worked those hours."

"You did," Nevaeh said. "And they taxed the hours anyway. Welcome to being a person." She stole one of his fries with the calm entitlement of a shiftmate. "But also, think about it the other way. My grandma collects a Social Security check every month, like an annuity that the government sends her, and it's most of what she lives on. Somebody's twenty-one dollars is a piece of that. Mine, probably. Yours now, too, which is hilarious, because you have forty dollars total."

Dylan laughed despite himself. "I'm somebody's grandma's income stream."

"A tiny, tiny tributary," Israel said from across the counter, without looking up from the ketchup.

That night Ms. Hamdan found the placemat on table four, Dylan's arithmetic marching across the cartoon milkshake, and taped it to the kitchen wall beside the health inspection certificate, where it stayed like folk art. When he came in Saturday, she caught his eye and tapped the wall twice, and he felt embarrassingly proud, like a kid whose drawing got the refrigerator.

Later, during the dead stretch between lunch and dinner, he texted his mom, because it seemed like the kind of thing she'd have opinions about. "my check was short 49 bucks but it's social security, 6.2 percent, israel explained it. also if you ever make a ton of money they stop taking it past some yearly wage cap. rich people." Her reply came while he was scraping the flattop, the phone buzzing in his apron pocket. "Welcome to the working class, sweetheart. Also you owe me for last month's gas, which conveniently has no wage limit."

He smiled at the grill, at its obsolescent dials that only Ms. Hamdan understood, and texted back, "deducted from my annuity." Then he flipped the last burger, slid it onto a bun, and hollered toward the counter, "Order up, Israel, before it gets any sadder."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
story:
The food bank operated out of the common room of Birchwood Manor, a seniors' residence on the east side of town, and Vincent arrived at nine sharp because the scholarship application required forty documented volunteer hours and he intended to document every one of them. Ms. Clarke, who ran the operation from a folding table wedged between a piano nobody played and a wall of fake ferns, handed him a hairnet and a pair of gloves and pointed at a tower of grocery bags. "Sort," she said. "Cereal with cereal, cans with cans, anything damaged or open goes in the bin. And Vincent, no heroics."

Raquel, who had apparently done this before and had the bored competence of someone who had, was already halfway through her own bag. "Ignore her," she said. "The heroics are the fun part. Last month a guy found a can of pumpkin from 2011 and we made it a whole ceremony." Tianna, sorting beside her, held up a jar of pickles and peered at it like a jeweler. "This one's from my church," she said. "Which means some auntie donated the contents of her panic closet."

Vincent got to work. The bags smelled of other people's kitchens, onion powder and damp cardboard, and the residents of Birchwood Manor drifted past the folding tables in slow orbits, offering commentary. An old man in a cardigan stopped to inform him that canned beans were a scam. A woman with a walker rated each cereal box aloud, docking points for anything with a cartoon mascot. "Gratuitous," she said of a toucan in sunglasses, and moved on.

The problem arrived in the third bag. Five cans of soup, sealed, labels intact, each stamped with a best before date nine days past. Vincent held one up to the window light, turned it over, and felt the pleasing weight of a decision. Rules were rules; damaged or open went in the bin; the date was neither. But a date was a date, and he had a vision of some family eating questionable soup because he'd been squeamish about a garbage can. He stacked all five by the bin, then unstacked them, then stacked three and held two, which was when he understood he had no idea what he was doing and no principle to hide behind.

"Raquel," he said. "These are past the date. Do I toss them?"

She came over, read the cans, and shrugged. "Those are fine. A best before date just marks when the quality might start to drop, not when it becomes unsafe. Sealed cans past it can still be safe to eat." She said it the way she said everything, like the information owed her money, and went back to her bag.

Vincent stood there recalibrating. His whole life, the date on a carton had functioned as law, and it turned out to be closer to a rumor. "So the milk thing too?" he asked. "No, don't tell me, I don't want to become one of those people with opinions about milk." Tianna laughed so hard she had to put down the pickles. "He's having a crisis," she announced to the room, and the woman with the walker said, "Good, it's about time somebody did."

He put the soup in the good pile. It felt, briefly, like a triumph of reason over reflex, though he was honest enough with himself to notice how much of the triumph was just Raquel's shrug doing the work. He'd accepted her claim in four seconds without checking anything, which was the same reflex wearing a nicer shirt. Somewhere his philosophy teacher had a word for this, a whole unit on how you know what you know, epistemology, and Vincent had written a test on it and gotten an A without once applying it to soup. He decided that if Raquel was wrong, he was at least wrong efficiently, and that this did not entirely assuage him.

At noon the residents were served sandwiches that the volunteers had assembled, and the old man in the cardigan sat across from Vincent and said, "You put that soup back. I saw you." Vincent waited for a verdict. "Used to be a grocer," the man said. "Threw out a lot of perfectly good food because the trucks were late and the dates were wrong. Whole pallets." He bit his sandwich, chewed, and looked at Vincent with something that might have been approval or might have been appetite. "You want the last word on it, ask the soup," he said. "Open it and smell it. That's the whole science."

Vincent looked over at the good pile, where the five cans sat among the others, indistinguishable now from everything that was certainly fine, and Tianna called from the pickle station, "Don't listen to him, he's about to make you open one."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts.
story:
Mr. Gallagher had written one word in the margin of Victor's draft, underlined twice where his thesis sentence should have been: "Fact?" Victor had stared at it through last period, and now he was staring at it again, the draft flattened against the small table by the window of the cafe, a cold cappuccino beside it and Erika across from him eating a croissant in deliberate, unhurried bites.

"Read it to me," she said.

"'The Civilian Conservation Corps planted over three billion trees between 1933 and 1942,'" Victor read. "'This paper will discuss the CCC.'"

"And he wrote 'Fact?'"

"And a question mark. Which is worse, somehow. Like he's disappointed in me." Victor turned the page over as though the answer might be printed on the back. "I did everything else. I have fourteen sources. I collated them all into a bibliography, alphabetical, hanging indents, the whole thing. Chicago style. Footnotes. I spent a whole Sunday on the footnotes."

Erika brushed a flake of pastry off her sleeve. "So ask him what's wrong with it."

"I did. He said, 'Tell me what you're arguing.' Which is not an answer."

Mikaela arrived then, dropping her bag onto the third chair, apologizing for the bus, stealing a corner of Erika's croissant without asking. She pulled out her own draft, which had a B+ in red pencil at the top, and set it beside Victor's like an exhibit. Her thesis was underlined in pencil, not questioned: "The CCC's tree-planting program succeeded as public relations but failed as conservation, because monoculture planting weakened the forests it claimed to save."

Victor read it twice. "You're allowed to say that?"

"I'm allowed to argue it. That's the difference. Gallagher told us the first week. A thesis has to be arguable. Something a reasonable person could actually dispute."

"Nobody reasonable disputes that the CCC planted trees," Erika said slowly, working it out. "It's just true. It's in the encyclopedia."

"Right. So it can't be a thesis." Mikaela said it the way she said most things, as though it had been obvious to her for years. "You can't write a paper proving the sky is blue. There's nowhere to go."

Victor sat back. The cafe's window was fogged at the corners, and beyond it the street was doing its ordinary late-afternoon business, a man hosing down the sidewalk, two kids fighting over a single scooter. He felt something shift, not seismic exactly, but close enough, a small tectonic slide in his understanding of what he'd been doing for three weeks. He had thought the assignment was about gathering. Fourteen sources, thirty notecards, a folder on his desktop named CCC FINAL that was, he now saw, a pile of information with no engine in it.

"So the paper's not a container," he said. "It's a fight."

"It's a position," Mikaela said. "You take a side and defend it with the evidence. The footnotes aren't the building. They're the scaffolding."

"But I don't have a side." The admission came out smaller than he intended. "Everything I read, the tree planting worked. Or it didn't. The sources disagree with each other, not with me."

"That's where the side comes from," Erika said, and pointed her fork at his notecards, which he had begun spreading across the table like a poor man's tarot. "Look. Put the ones that say it worked over there. The ones that say it failed there. What's left in your hand?"

Victor collated the cards into two uneven stacks, biting his lip, ignoring the waitress who wanted to know if they were ordering anything else. The "worked" stack was taller. But when he fanned through the smaller one, he found the article from the forestry journal, the one he'd skipped past because it was dense and annoying, about erosion data that didn't match the program's own reporting. He read the abstract again, properly this time.

"Okay," he said. "Okay. Here's something. The CCC counted trees planted. That was the number everybody celebrated. But planting a tree and growing a forest aren't the same thing, and nobody measured survival. So maybe, 'The CCC's tree-planting succeeded by the measures it set for itself but those measures were chosen for publicity, not for conservation.'" He looked up. "Is that arguable?"

"It's arguable," Mikaela said.

"Is it true?"

"That's the fight. You find out." She was already packing her bag, late for her shift. "That's the whole point. That's why it's a paper and not a poster."

After she left, Erika ordered them both hot chocolates, on her, because he looked like a person who had been through something. Victor wrote the new thesis at the top of a clean page, crossed it out, rewrote it, crossed out only the second clause, and kept the third version. He knew, in an honest corner of himself, that he didn't yet know if he could defend it. The survival data might exist somewhere clean and complete, in which case his argument would dissolve into someone else's fact. Or it might not exist at all, in which case he would have to argue from absence, which sounded like the kind of thing that got a "Fact?" of its own. He would go to the library Saturday. He would email the forestry professor in Oregon whose name kept appearing in the footnotes, the real ones, the ones already doing the fighting.

For now there was a detente between him and the assignment, a quiet laying down of arms on both sides. He wasn't winning yet. He might not win. But the paper had a position now, and the position had him.

He turned the draft over to the blank side and wrote, at the top, "What I'm actually arguing," and underlined it twice.

"Why twice?" Erika asked.

"That's how many he gave me."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Sugar bloom is a dry, gritty white coating caused when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries.
story:
Sophie had planned to spend Saturday afternoon being gloomy about her college rejection letter, but Blake's text had said, in its entirety, "chocolate. my kitchen. bring your nerd brain," and it was hard to stay gloomy about anything at a person who punctuated with nothing.

"You said you wanted to learn this," Blake said, sliding a marble slab across the counter like a bartender in a film about bartenders. "Zackary's coming, by the way. He promised to be decorative and quiet."

"That promise has a success rate of zero," Sophie said, but she was already chopping the chocolate, which was the first thing the video had taught her: chop fine, reserve a third, melt the rest to precisely body temperature. The video's instructor, a garrulous woman with a copper pot and a habit of announcing aphorisms like "the chocolate knows when you doubt it," had gone on for forty minutes. Sophie had watched it twice and taken notes with the seriousness of someone preparing for a trial.

Zackary arrived twenty minutes late with a bag of clementines and no explanation. He stationed himself at the kitchen table and narrated. "She's stirring it. Now she's stirring it slower. Now she's checking the thermometer like it owes her money."

"Und temper" was how the instructor had described a chocolate that hadn't been agitated enough, and Sophie could feel the possibility of it hovering over her like weather. She poured the melted chocolate onto the cool marble and worked it with a spatula, spreading and gathering, spreading and gathering, watching the gloss change as the temperature fell. Blake held the thermometer and called out numbers like a coxswain. When they hit the target, they stirred the reserved chocolate back in, and the mixture went liquid and bright, a lacquered brown that looked almost wet.

"Test it," Blake said, and Sophie smeared a little on parchment paper and waited, hands hovering. Mr. Gupta, the neighbour, had wandered in halfway through, drawn by the smell, and now stood by the window fanning himself with a newspaper and offering commentary on humidity, which nobody had asked for. "It's like a swamp out there today," he said cheerfully. "My windows are sweating. My newspaper is sweating."

Blake watched Sophie peel the test smear off the parchment and snap it beside her ear. It broke with a clean, high click, like a knuckle, and the broken edge was matte and even. Sophie's whole face did something complicated and pleased. "That's tempered," she said. "Shiny and it snaps. That's the whole thing. That's it."

They poured the chocolate into the molds Blake had dug out of a cupboard, tapped out the bubbles, and then hit the problem: where to set it. The counter was warm from the afternoon, so Zackary, with the confidence of a man who had never once tempered anything, opened the fridge and slid the tray in. "Cold makes things hard," he said. "This is known."

Sophie had a feeling about this, a small unease she couldn't source, and she said so, but the fridge was already humming shut and Mr. Gupta was offering everyone clementines, and the argument calcified into a joke about Zackary's contributions to food science. Twenty minutes later they pulled the tray out into the swampy kitchen, and the tops of the chocolates, which had gone glossy and firm in the cold, began within minutes to dull. Sophie leaned over them and touched one with a fingertip. Where she'd touched, the surface came away slightly gritty, a pale dry smear, and as the chocolates warmed further, a powdery white bloom crept across the tops like frost that had changed its mind about being pretty.

"That's not how it looked in the video," Blake said flatly, bending close. "The video never did that."

Sophie got her notebook and flipped, and there it was in her own handwriting from two nights ago, a line she'd written down without really believing she'd need it. She read it aloud. "Sugar bloom. A dry, gritty white coating. Moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface, then the sugar recrystallizes as it dries." She looked up. "We took cold chocolate out into Mr. Gupta's sweating windows. The cold chocolates pulled moisture out of the humid air, the moisture dissolved sugar off the surface, and when it dried, the sugar came back as crystals." She touched the powdery top again, rubbed her fingers together. "Gritty. Exactly gritty."

"So the fridge betrayed us," Zackary said. "Noted. I will never trust anything again."

"The fridge was fine," Sophie said. "The fridge plus this kitchen was the problem." She stood there with her gritty fingers and her notebook and her half-thought, which she assembled out loud because that was how she did it. "The video wanted everything controlled, room temperature, patience, and that's one way to think. But Zackary's way, cold makes things hard, that's not wrong either, it's just incomplete." She looked at the ruined tray and then at the bowl, where a little tempered chocolate still sat, holding its gloss in the warm kitchen like it had opinions. "You have to hold both. Cool it, yes, but cool it somewhere dry, and let it set before it meets the air."

"Is that an aphorism?" Blake asked. "Because if you're doing aphorisms now, I want it on record that mine was better."

"Yours was 'chocolate, my kitchen, bring your nerd brain,'" Sophie said, already re-melting a pot of water underneath a clean bowl. "History will decide."

Mr. Gupta peeled a clementine in one unbroken spiral and said nothing, which for him was a kind of applause. Sophie wiped the molds clean, poured the remaining chocolate fresh from the bowl, and set the new tray on the marble slab, away from the window, away from the fridge. Then she sat down across from Zackary, chin in her hand, and they all three watched it set, slowly, in the warm and humid and entirely uncontrolled afternoon.

"If these bloom too," Zackary said, "I'm eating the evidence."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Many driving courses teach keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness.
story:
The bus shelter on Corbett Street had become Jackson's office, in a manner of speaking, because it was the one place where Mr. Van Dijk would sit still long enough to talk about driving. Mr. Van Dijk lived three doors down, had driven lorries for forty years, and refused every attempt Jackson's mother made to press money on him. "A retired man who takes an honorarium for teaching a neighbour's boy," he said, folding his arms, "is a retired man who has run out of better things to do with his mornings." So the arrangement stayed informal: twice a week, in the dusty Corolla with the soft passenger brake, and afterward a debrief at the bus stop while the Number 14 hissed past without stopping for either of them.

The test was in eleven days, and the test had two parts, and Jackson could do exactly one of them. Parallel parking he had come to understand as a kind of argument with geometry, one he was slowly winning. Merging onto the ring road was different. Merging required him to be two people at once, one watching the ramp ahead and one watching the mirror, and neither person trusted the other yet.

"You count like a man confessing sins," Mr. Van Dijk said that Thursday, after the third aborted merge. They had pulled over on the shoulder of the on-ramp, hazards ticking, and sat looking at the traffic streaming past at highway speed. "Far too fast, all of it, so it means nothing."

"You told me to count."

"I told you to count two seconds. The car ahead passes a sign, you say the seconds, and if you pass the same sign before two, you are too close. That is the whole science. Two seconds at least, and you give more when the rain comes, or snow, or it is dark." He tapped the windshield, where a thin drizzle had begun to bead. "So today, what do you think?"

"More," Jackson said. "It's wet."

"It is wet. So you count longer and you leave more room, and you let them honk."

Youssef and Francis found him at the bus stop afterward, both of them freshly licensed, both of them insufferable about it. Francis had passed on his second attempt and had theories about examiners, about which testing centre was softer, about how the real trick of driving was confidence. "You hesitate on a merge, you fail," Francis said, leaning against the timetable glass. "You just go. The gap opens up if you commit."

"That's not how it works," Jackson said.

"It's how it worked for me."

Youssef, who had failed once himself, said nothing for a while, which was Youssef's way of disagreeing. Then he said, "The first time, I did what Francis says. Committed to a gap that wasn't there. The examiner grabbed the wheel and we ended up on the verge, and she said, very calmly, that we would be going back to the centre now." He turned his tea in his hands. "The second time I counted. Two seconds, and it was raining that day so I made it three. I merged like an old man and I passed. I have decided to be an old man."

Jackson laughed, but he kept thinking about it on the walk home, and again the next morning, which was Saturday, when Mr. Van Dijk took him out at dusk because, as he put it, Jackson's habits were too diurnal and examiners did not check whether you were a morning person. The light failed early and the drizzle thickened, and by the time they reached the on-ramp the windshield was a smear of orange from the sodium lamps. Jackson signalled, checked the mirror, found the reference, a pale road sign, and watched the car ahead pass it.

"One thousand and one. One thousand and two. One thousand and three." His own car crept past the sign well after the third second, and for the first time the distance behind felt like something he owned rather than something that had simply happened to him. He picked his gap, held his speed steady instead of stabbing at the pedal, and slid into the stream of traffic so smoothly that Mr. Van Dijk said nothing at all, which Jackson was learning to read as the highest available praise.

He still did not know if he would pass. Francis's certainty and Youssef's caution had both gone into him and neither had won; what he had instead was something with less shape, a rule he could count on and a decision he would still have to make in the moment, alone, with an examiner's clipboard resting on her knees. But at the bus stop on Monday, waiting for the Number 14, he found himself watching the car in front of him pass the shelter and counting under his breath, one thousand and one, one thousand and two, and when he reached the shelter himself the space still lay open behind him, patient and sufficient. Mr. Van Dijk, waiting beside him with his hands in his pockets, said, "Again."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
Brooke chose the table by the microfiche cabinets because nobody sat there anymore, and she spread her folder of college printouts across it like evidence. The library's February light came through the high windows in a flat gray sheet. She opened her laptop, logged into the Common Application, and stared at the activity list she had rewritten four times: cross country, two years; the pharmacy job, eighteen months; the essay draft that still began with a sentence she hated.

Winston dropped into the chair opposite her without asking. "You done yet?"

"Almost." She turned the screen a few degrees away from him.

"You said almost in November." He peeled the cover off a muffin he'd smuggled past the front desk. "My cousin did twenty separate applications back in the day. Before all this. Twenty essays, twenty fees."

"It didn't used to be like this?"

"The Common App," he said. "It started in 1975 with fifteen member colleges. Now it's over a thousand."

She looked at him over the top of the screen. "How do you know that?"

"I read things. Occasionally." He shrugged. "Anyway, you're lucky. One application, all your schools. My cousin hand-typed every page."

Brooke sat with that for a moment. Fifteen colleges in 1975, over a thousand now, and somewhere in between, the thing on her laptop had become a door that opened onto everywhere at once. She had been treating it like a corridor with one exit.

Emeric arrived next, hood up, earbuds around his neck, and set down a stack of returned books he was supposed to be shelving. "Mr. Suryanto's looking for you, Winston. You left the carts again."

"In a minute." Winston leaned toward Brooke. "Just submit it."

"It's not a platitude situation. 'Just submit it' doesn't help."

"It's not a platitude if it's literally the next action."

Emeric pulled out the chair at the end of the table and sat, which meant he was allowed ten more minutes of hiding before it counted as ditching. "What's the holdup?"

She hadn't said it out loud to anyone. "My essay. It's about my mom's store closing. And I keep thinking, what if the admissions person reads it and thinks I'm doing the sad story thing. Using her." She kept her voice even. "But it's also just true. It's what happened."

"Then it's what happened," Emeric said.

"That easy?"

"No. But it's still what happened."

Behind them, the printer hummed, and Mr. Suryanto came around the reference desk with the unhurried gait of a man who had worked in this building longer than any of them had been alive. He did not mention the carts. He looked at the spread of printouts, the laptop, the half-eaten muffin, and said only, "The library closes at nine. You have three hours."

After he'd passed, Brooke minimized the essay and opened the member list instead, scrolling past school after school, state universities and small colleges and places she'd never heard of in states she couldn't picture. Over a thousand. She'd applied to nine and thought of it as enormous, a spread of bets, and now the list made nine look like almost nothing, like standing in a station and boarding the first train that came.

"I'm going to add one," she said.

Winston stopped chewing. "You're what."

"A school that doesn't need the essay to be perfect. Somewhere with a good program, not a famous name." She had been circumspect about the reach schools, hedging every line of the application in case the readers saw through her. This one she could just answer. "My mom keeps saying I should decide already. I keep saying I'm deciding. But really I've been waiting to be told."

"You can't know if it's right," Emeric said. "Before you go."

"I know." That was the part nobody's advice covered. She could introspect for another month, another year, and the answer would still arrive incomplete, a best guess dressed up as a plan. Winston's cousin had typed twenty applications and ended up at one school, one life. The odds had changed; the not-knowing hadn't.

She opened the essay, deleted the first sentence, and typed a new one, plainer, about the morning her mother taped the closing notice to the register and kept making change while customers read it. Then she filled in the new school's supplement, her answers getting shorter and more direct with each box. Winston watched over his muffin without comment. Emeric checked the clock.

She hovered over the submit button, and her hand stayed there a second longer than necessary, and then she pressed it. The confirmation bar filled and the screen asked if she wanted to view her other applications.

"Not yet," she said, and closed the lid.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Alexa's grandmother had claimed the long table nearest the tent poles at the Sephardic Heritage Street Festival, which meant the whole family was folded into the community Seder whether they had planned on it or not. Alexa had planned on it not. She had planned on finding Violet and Anissa near the ferris wheel, where the festival stopped being synagogue-adjacent and started being just a festival, with fried dough and a band tuning up badly.

"Sit," her grandmother said, and Alexa sat, arranging her skirt over the folding chair with the resignation of someone who understood that her family operated as an oligarchy: whichever three aunts were loudest held all the power, and the rest of the population voted by staying quiet.

The problem revealed itself before the soup did. Her little cousin Theo, seven years old and pale as the tablecloth, was supposed to ask the Four Questions. Alexa only knew this because she had overheard her uncle drilling him behind the pastry stall, choleric and hissing, "Again, from the top," while Theo's voice shrank to nothing. Now Theo sat two seats down, staring at the Haggadah in front of him like it might bite.

"We have a situation," Anissa said, materializing beside the table with Violet behind her. Violet was eating fried dough already, which Alexa found almost heroic under the circumstances.

"The situation is my cousin," Alexa said. "He has to ask the Four Questions, and he's going to freeze, and then my uncle is going to freeze, and then the whole tent."

"Why does the littlest kid have to do it?" Violet asked, licking sugar off her thumb.

"That's just how it works," Alexa said. "The youngest one there asks them. It starts with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?' Theo knows it cold, he told me last week, but knowing it cold and saying it in front of eighty people are different animals."

Anissa lowered herself into the empty chair at the end, uninvited but unbothered. "So coach him. You're good at that. You coached me before the debate semifinal and I didn't throw up, which was a first."

"You also refused to problematize your own argument, which is why you lost," Alexa said, but she was already watching Theo, who had begun folding his napkin into smaller and smaller squares.

She excused herself from the table, which cost her one sharp look from an aunt, and crouched next to Theo's chair. "Hey. Walk with me."

"We're not supposed to leave," Theo whispered.

"We're going to the pastry stall and back. That's not leaving, that's orbiting." She steered him past Ms. Yilmaz's table, where their neighbor was arranging glasses of mint tea, and Ms. Yilmaz called out, "Alexa! Your uncle's been interrogating that poor boy like he owes him money."

"Working on it," Alexa said, and kept walking. Behind the stall, in the gap between the tent wall and a parked truck, she crouched to Theo's level. "Forget the tent. Forget everyone. Who's your audience going to be?"

"Theo," she said, "this is the part I actually know. In debate, you don't perform for the crowd. You talk to the judge. There is no crowd. There's just one person you're telling something true." She pointed at herself. "I'm the judge. Ask me."

He gripped the truck's bumper with both hands. "Why is this night different from all other nights?"

"Because on all other nights we eat any kind of bread, and tonight only matzah," Alexa answered, and then, "Wait. I'm not supposed to answer. I'm just supposed to listen. I'm your aunt with bad posture. Go again."

He went again. Then a third time, and the fourth time something loosened in his voice, the words coming out in a rhythm instead of a stumble. Violet and Anissa appeared at the mouth of the gap, and Violet, holding the Haggadah she'd swiped from Alexa's seat, prompted him in a stage whisper when he faltered on the second question. He didn't falter on the third.

When they walked back in, the soup was arriving and the tent was loud. The rabbi tapped her glass. Theo stood, and Alexa stood too, halfway, before she caught herself and sat back down. He didn't look at the eighty people. He looked at the gap between Anissa and Violet, where Alexa was sitting, and asked why this night was different from all other nights, all four times, in a voice that reached the far poles of the tent.

Later, with the ferris wheel lit up beyond the tent flaps and her aunts arguing about whether to leave before the band started, Alexa found she wasn't in any hurry. "Next year you'll have to fight someone younger for the job," she told Theo, and he looked around the table, counting heads.

"There's nobody younger."

"There will be," Anissa said, tearing a piece of matzah in half and handing the larger piece to Alexa. "Families are like that."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming.
story:
Charlotte arrived at the farmers' market at six-forty with a double boiler in a canvas bag and her mother's thermometer rolled in a dish towel. Ms. Pritchard's stall stood at the end of the second row, between the honey table and a man selling cut dahlias, and behind it, on the folding table, lay a slab of marble the size of a door. Charlotte had called twice in June asking to apprentice, and each time Ms. Pritchard had said the same thing: come early, before the customers, and we will see what your hands know.

"We will see" turned out to mean two hours of folding boxes and weighing cacao while Ms. Pritchard sold to the early regulars. At eight, when the rush thinned, Ms. Pritchard melted a bowl of dark chocolate over warm water and handed Charlotte a spatula. "I want it shiny," Charlotte said. "It has to snap when you break it." Ms. Pritchard only nodded toward the marble.

The first attempt failed in the bowl. Charlotte had kept the chocolate moving, had watched the thermometer climb, and had poured it into the molds anyway, because the numbers looked right to her. Her mother, a lab technician, ran a kitchen like a protocol, and Charlotte had inherited the faith that if you measured a thing correctly, it behaved. The bars set dull. When she turned one out and bent it, it bent, pale streaks blooming across the surface like frost on a window. Ms. Pritchard picked up a streaked bar, snapped it, got nothing, and set it down without comment that could be called bellicose, though her eyebrows did some work.

Elizabeth and Maude appeared at half past nine, ostensibly to buy bread, actually to loiter. Elizabeth had been accepted early to a chemistry program and considered herself, in her own words, the tempering authority, having read four articles the night before. "It's crystallization," she announced, leaning over the bowl. "Five crystal forms and only one of them is the good one, but nobody agrees on the temperatures." Maude, who worked weekends at her family's restaurant and had watched a pastry chef do this a hundred times, snorted. "You don't need a thermometer," she said. "You need the stone. What he does is called tabling. You spread the chocolate out on the marble and work it around until it cools down and starts setting right, then you get it into the molds fast." Charlotte looked from one to the other, Elizabeth citing precision, Maude citing practice, and felt the two positions settle in her like weights on opposite pans.

She tempered the chocolate again over the warm water, then poured half of it onto the marble slab. The stone had been sitting in the shade since dawn and it was cool enough that the chocolate made a soft sound as it landed, thicker than liquid. She spread it flat with the spatula, scraped it back into the center, spread it again, and kept working it, back and forth, the way Maude had described and the way she could suddenly see in her own memory of a video she'd watched and dismissed. The chocolate began to thicken under the spatula. Elizabeth held the thermometer over the pool without touching it and called out the falling temperature like a scorekeeper. On her mother's view, Charlotte thought, this was chaos, no controlled variable anywhere; on Maude's, it was just what hands did. She kept spreading and gathering, and somewhere in the third minute she stopped waiting for the two views to fight it out and simply attended to the chocolate, which was doing something she could feel but not name.

When it had thickened to the texture of thick batter, she scraped it back into the bowl with the warmer chocolate and stirred. Ms. Pritchard, who had been selling to a woman with dahlias now wrapped in newspaper, came back and looked into the bowl without touching it. "Now," she said. Charlotte poured. The chocolate ran off the spatula in a ribbon that folded on itself like fabric, and she tapped each mold twice against the table and slid them onto the tray.
